turns.zh: 大致的结构是怎样的？如果有人想了解这些是怎么运作的，如果他们想在我们聊的过程中加入，它们怎么运作？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Okay, so you apply at phyl.org, P-H-Y-L, Phyl with a Y. Again, it's free. We match you behind the scenes. Now, when you apply, we ask, "First of all, are you in a job and looking or are you out of work?" Because we separate those two because they have different cadences. If you're in a job and looking, we call you a slow seeker because you have a full-time job and you can't work as quickly. If you're out of work and looking, we call you a fast seeker and we put you in different groups. Fast seeker or slow seeker. We also ask though, are you willing to be a moderator? Every council needs a moderator, and every moderator is a job seeker who volunteers to do that. If you volunteer to moderate, first of all, you get matched faster, and secondly, you get more training and support. (00:11:18): It's a little bit more work for a lot more benefit. We've gotten 2,000 moderators, Lenny, it's amazing. And we feel like we're just beginning. So you apply, you get matched, and then you go through an orientation program that we run live where we tell you how this works and what to expect in your first meeting. And then there's a whole set of agendas and materials and everything in the book as well as everyone gets a free workbook, a 100-page workbook after they join the community with all of the templates and guides and questions. And then the moderator pulls you together, you work on Zoom or whatever technology, it's remote typically. And you do a first meeting, we call it meeting zero, where you're open and vulnerable. People share stories about their lives and who they are, builds trust and get a sense of who people are. And then you move into the process. You meet twice a week typically if you're in a fast seeker council and every two weeks if you're in a slow seeker. So that's the start of the answer. Does that help you think?
turns.zh: 好，你在 phyl.org 申请，P-H-Y-L，带 Y 的 Phyl。再次强调，免费。我们在幕后匹配你。申请时我们会问："首先，你是在职求职，还是已经失业？"因为这两类人节奏不同，我们把他们分开。如果你在职求职，我们叫你"慢速求职者"（slow seeker），因为你有一份全职工作，没法那么快。如果你失业求职，我们叫你"快速求职者"（fast seeker），把你放进不同的组。快速或慢速。我们还问：你愿意当协调人（moderator）吗？每个委员会都需要一个协调人，而每个协调人都是自愿做这件事的求职者。如果你自愿协调，首先你匹配得更快，其次你得到更多培训和支持。(00:11:18)：多一点工作，换很多倍的收益。我们已经有了 2,000 个协调人，Lenny，太不可思议了。而且我们觉得才刚刚开始。所以你申请、被匹配，然后参加我们现场运行的入职项目，告诉你这怎么运作、第一次会议该期待什么。然后书里有一整套议程、材料，每个人加入社区后还会得到一本免费的、100 页的工作手册，里面有所有模板、指南和问题。然后协调人把大家聚起来，你们在 Zoom 或任何技术上工作，通常是远程。你们开第一次会议，我们叫"第零次会议"（meeting zero），你要开放、脆弱。人们分享自己生活的故事和他们是怎样的人，建立信任、了解彼此。然后你进入流程。如果你是快速求职者委员会，通常每周见两次；慢速求职者每两周一次。这就是答案的开头。这对你思考有帮助吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, really helpful. And then you basically are on this council until you find a job, I imagine.
turns.zh: 对，很有帮助。那我猜你基本上就待在这个委员会里，直到找到工作。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you can share around the impact you've seen? The reason I reached out to you to come on this podcast is I just started seeing people mentioning that they found a job and maybe the thing that helped them most was your book and being on one of these councils. I imagine there's a lot of stories you hear and a lot of numbers you could see of just people succeeding going through, so what can you share about just the impact you've seen?
turns.zh: 你能分享一点你看到的 impact 吗？我联系你来上这档播客的原因，是我开始看到人们提到他们找到了工作，也许最能帮到他们的，就是你的书以及加入这些委员会之一。我想你听到过很多故事、也看到过很多数字，关于人们成功走完这个过程，所以你能分享些什么关于你看到的 impact？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Well, I posted on LinkedIn today that I was going to be on your podcast and I asked people if they wanted to share stories with me, and over email and LinkedIn, I've been flooded with stories from people who are in the process or people who did it. If you like, I can pull up and share a few of those if that would be helpful.
turns.zh: 嗯，我今天在 LinkedIn 上发帖说我要上你的播客，问大家愿不愿意跟我分享故事，结果通过邮件和 LinkedIn 我被那些正在过程中、或已经完成的人发来的故事淹没了。如果你愿意，我可以调出几个分享一下，如果有帮助的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, if there's a few you have there, that'd be really sweet.
turns.zh: 好啊，如果你那儿有几个，那就太好了。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Okay, so Justin Meats is a chief product officer who's gone through the process and he posted on LinkedIn today. He said, "As a product leader, I love how it has you apply the product process to your career." This comes out of the product world, it's a product lens on the job search, and it's for everyone, but it really makes sense for product people. And he says, "Not only does your JSC help bounce ideas and help your job search, they also help you keep going and accountable when you're low on emotional energy." (00:13:46): I talk about this in the book, Lenny, I say, "Look, most people think, 'What's the most important thing to manage during your job search?'" They think, well, maybe it's their resume or LinkedIn profile or their ability to network or candidate market fit, a concept I introduced I think is really important. All those things are really important, but the most important thing to manage is your emotional balance. I talk about your emotional balance sheet. And for many job seekers, they have more liabilities than assets on their old balance sheets. They have more fear and anxiety, they feel demoralized, they have a hard time going. That's why these things are so important. (00:14:24): He also says, "Hey, it's a journey, and the more you embrace it, the more you learn about yourself." And he says... and this is important Lenny. I don't have a magic wand that especially in a down market today that magically gets a job. It's hard. The job search, it can be hard and humiliating at times. I know. This is why I want to create this community, why we're doing this. We want to give you a place where you can really get the support when it's hard and humiliating. But the process will ultimately set you up for success if you follow it. (00:14:58): This one woman who just started, she's a senior product leader in a major financial institution, and she said she couldn't believe the level of support and openness and vulnerability. We really emphasize people being open and vulnerable, and I've learned a lot about how to create that environment. It ties back to asking for help, which I know we'll talk about more at some point. But when you create that, it's amazing what people can do together, Lenny. Amazing.
turns.zh: 好，Justin Meats 是一位经历过这个流程的首席产品官，他今天在 LinkedIn 上发了帖。他说："作为一个产品领导者，我超爱它让你把产品流程应用到你的职业上。"这来自产品世界，它是求职上的产品视角，它适合每个人，但对产品人特别说得通。他说："你的 JSC（求职委员会）不仅帮你碰撞想法、帮你的求职，还在你情绪低落、能量不足时帮你坚持下去、保持责任感。"(00:13:46)：我在书里聊这个，Lenny，我说："看，大多数人想，'求职时最重要管理的是什么？'"他们想，也许是简历、LinkedIn 主页、社交能力，或者我提出的、我认为很重要的概念——候选人市场契合。这些都重要，但最重要的是管理你的情绪平衡（emotional balance）。我谈你的"情绪资产负债表"（emotional balance sheet）。对很多求职者来说，他们旧资产负债表上的负债比资产多。他们有更多的恐惧和焦虑，感到泄气，很难前行。这就是为什么这些事如此重要。(00:14:24)：他还说："嘿，这是一段旅程，你越拥抱它，就越了解自己。"他说……这很重要，Lenny。我没有魔杖，尤其是在今天这个下行市场，能神奇地让人找到工作。这很难。求职，有时会很难、很屈辱。我知道。这就是我想创建这个社区、我们做这个的原因。我们想给你一个地方，在艰难和屈辱时能真正得到支持。但如果你遵循这个流程，它最终会让你走向成功。(00:14:58)：有个刚起步的女性，是一家大型金融机构的高级产品领导者，她说她不敢相信那种支持、开放和脆弱的程度。我们真的很强调人们开放和脆弱，而我也学到很多怎么营造那种环境。这和寻求帮助有关，我知道我们某个时候会更多聊到。但当你创造出那种环境，人们在一起能做的事太神奇了，Lenny。太神奇了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to reinforce this point, people listening may be like, "I'm just going to keep looking for a job. I'll use all this advice. I don't need a group." What's your best pitch, again, to help people see the value of doing this in a group and joining a council or starting a council?
turns.zh: 就为了强调这一点，听的人可能会想："我就继续自己找工作好了。我会用上所有这些建议。我不需要小组。"你最好的推销、再一次帮人们看到在小组里、加入或发起一个委员会的价值，是什么？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: I acknowledge that that's a reaction that some people have. That's totally valid. This is unusual, what we're doing here. This is not how people look for a job. We're trying to disrupt the job search process. Lenny, this is my quick story. We had a great interview with a couple. Two of them were product leaders. They had met at Amazon and then had gone to have great careers. They both got laid off. The woman joined a Job Search Council right away. She loved it, she raved about it. Her husband, who was also an engineer, was a little more introverted. He's like, "Ah, this isn't for me." She said, "No, listen, you won't... " And finally he read the book. Because the book, it works for the product mind and for the engineering mind, it makes sense. He said, "I'll join a council, but I'm not going to be field connected to people. But I'll do this because you asked me to." (00:16:43): He sat in the interview, we have it up on the side, he was like, "Oh my God, I couldn't believe it. The level of trust we created right off the bat I've never experienced in my life. It's really truly accountability, the motivation, the ability to hang in there." And so I say to people, " Look, try it." We have all these videos on our website with all these people talking. Go look at it. If you want to read the book first and see if you think this makes sense. But try it. You will be shocked in a positive way. You'll discover how delightful it is. (00:17:25): We live in a world where there's increasing loneliness, Lenny. There's so much research about this, the Surgeon General's book, everybody talking about... And it's more detrimental to our health than smoking cigarettes. Bowling Alone famously came out 25 years ago. We live in a world where people have not experienced community in a powerful way. I don't mean message boards, I mean real community. And I think you have a sense of this because you do real community. And that's what we're talking about here. It's real community but with some practical tools and techniques, which we'll talk about. What do you think? Is that a good response to the-
turns.zh: 我承认那是一些人的反应。那完全合理。我们正在做的这事不寻常。这不是人们找工作的方式。我们想颠覆求职流程。Lenny，这是我的小故事。我们采访过一对很棒的夫妻。他们俩都是产品领导者。他们在 Amazon 相识，然后都有了很棒的职业。两人都被裁了。妻子立刻加入了一个求职委员会。她爱死了，赞不绝口。她丈夫也是工程师，更内向一点。他说："啊，这不适合我。"她说："不，听我说，你不会……"最后他读了这本书。因为这本书对产品脑和产业脑都说得通。他说："我会加入一个委员会，但我不会和人有很深的连接。但我做这个是因为你让我做的。"(00:16:43)：他坐在面试里——我们有录像——他说："哦我的天，我不敢相信。我们一开始建立起来的信任程度，我这辈子从没体验过。那是真正的责任感、动力、坚持下去的能力。"所以我告诉人们："看，试试。"我们网站上有所有这些视频，各种人都在讲。去看看。如果你想先读书看看这有没有道理，也行。但试试。你会 positively 地大吃一惊。你会发现它多令人愉悦。(00:17:25)：我们生活在一个孤独感日益增长的世界，Lenny。有很多关于这个的研究，卫生局局长的书，大家都在聊……而且它比抽烟对健康更有害。《独自保龄球》（Bowling Alone）在 25 年前出了名。我们生活在一个人们没有以有力方式体验过社区的世界。我不是说留言板，我是说真正的社区。而我想你有点感觉，因为你做的是真正的社区。这就是我们聊的。它是真正的社区，但带有一些实用工具和技巧，我们待会儿会聊。你觉得？这是对那个问题不错的回应吗——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm sold. I don't need a job, but I want to join one. You also just had a really beautiful way of describing these programs as a safety net for people.
turns.zh: 我被说服了。我不需要工作，但我想加入一个。你刚刚还用一种很美的方式，把这些项目描述成人们的安全网。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Does that ring a bell?
turns.zh: 这让你想起什么吗？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: If we go up to the 30,000-foot level, what are we doing here? What's our mission? We're building a private safety net for all those who've been laid off or let go. Look, we're not going to do what the government does with unemployment insurance, we're never going to be able to do something like that. But the government's never going to be able to innovate around how to actually look for a job. That's where we come in. We are trying to build this. We talked about this earlier, Lenny, creative destruction is this economic concept that sits at the heart of capitalism. Creative destruction basically says, "Under capitalism, it's dynamic. New products and services displace or disrupt old products and services, companies and methods." It's why our economy has grown sixfold over the last a hundred years. It's remarkable. It's why we have this amazing multi-trillion dollar economy. But it comes with some negative unintended consequences, which is that people both in jobs and out of jobs, they're anxious and fearful. There's no program that addresses that. (00:19:20): That's what we're going after here. We're trying to be the solve for the unintended consequences of the thing that is so positive in many ways and that we as product people love because we get to build new products and displace old products. I'll just say one more thing. The reason you know this creative destruction works so well is if you compare our economy to the late Soviet Union's economy. They were a planned economy with no creative destruction. So there was no innovation, and eventually it just failed. It just collapsed. It's remarkable, this is a huge country with a massive military and nuclear weapons, but they couldn't make their economy work. Why? Because they didn't have this element. So it's something to celebrate, but as we celebrate it, we need to have something that addresses the negative unintended consequences. All of us who benefited from this, I think it's our duty to do something about it.
turns.zh: 如果我们上升到三万英尺的高度，我们在这里做什么？我们的使命是什么？我们在为所有被裁员或解雇的人，建立一个私人的安全网。看，我们不会去做政府用失业保险做的事，我们永远做不到那种程度。但政府永远无法在"怎么真正找工作"上创新。这正是我们切入的地方。我们之前聊过，Lenny，创造性破坏（creative destruction）是处于资本主义核心的经济概念。创造性破坏基本是说："在资本主义下，它是动态的。新产品和服务取代或颠覆旧的产品和服务、公司和方法。"这就是为什么我们的经济在过去一百年增长了六倍。太了不起了。这就是我们有这个惊人的数万亿美元经济的原因。但它带有一些负面的、非预期的后果，那就是在职和失业的人，都焦虑、恐惧。没有哪个项目解决这个问题。(00:19:20)：这正是我们要去做的。我们想成为那个解决"创造性破坏这东西在很多方面都极正面、而我们作为产品人热爱它、因为我们能打造新产品取代旧产品"的负面非预期后果的人。我只再说一点。你知道创造性破坏运作得这么好的原因，是拿我们的经济和晚期苏联的经济比。他们是计划经济，没有创造性破坏。所以没有创新，最终就失败了。就崩塌了。太了不起了，这是一个有庞大军队和核武器的大国，但他们没法让经济运转。为什么？因为他们没有这个要素。所以这是件值得庆祝的事，但当我们庆祝它时，我们需要有东西去解决那些负面的非预期后果。我们所有从这个中受益的人，我觉得有责任做点什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is beautiful. You're very good at this. Let's shift to talking about tactics. Let's talk about some of the things that you've shared. So you've mentioned things like candidate market fit, playing to win. Go wherever you want to go. Let's pick a few and then dive in.
turns.zh: 太美了。你很擅长这个。我们转到聊战术吧。聊聊你分享过的一些东西。你提到了候选人市场契合、为赢而战。你想从哪开始都行。我们挑几个深入。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Candidate market fit is probably the most important job search tactic in the book, aside from the Job Search Council, and it may be the thing I'm known for. When I die, they coin candidate market fit. So here's the thing, and this is why this is so important in a down market, when you're looking for a job, you're in a marketplace with supply and demand characteristics. So if there's a lot of supply, which there is right now in the tech world because there's been a lot of layoffs, the overall economy, there's been net job additions, Lenny, but those have been primarily in healthcare and government. There've been net job losses in tech. We could talk about why that is, but that's the world that we're in. (00:21:17): So let's say you're a director of product. Two years ago when the economy was great in tech and the job market was great in tech, you could probably get a VP of product role. What about today? Well, today your candidate market fit's been pushed down because there's a bunch of VPs of products who are going to take a director role. Guess what? That means you might not be able to get the director role you might need to get a senior manager role or whatever. Now, the important thing about this is it's not a personal segment about you. It's the marketplace. And that's what so many people today in their notes to me said, that it was such a relief for them. While it's hard to figure out your candidate market fit, it's also a relief to know it's not about you. (00:21:59): So what I ask people to do is the first radical step I ask them to take is to think about what they want and what they don't want. Now, you might not think that that's a radical step, Lenny, but most people don't do that. When they get laid off, they spray and pray. That's the typical, "Let me just... " Wait a minute, just take a moment. They're like, "Oh, don't slow me down." I'm like, "I'm going to slow you down to go fast." In fact, what our data shows is that the average job search in the Job Search Council from beginning to end is three months. If you look at the national data for job search, it's three to six months. So we are at the very low end of the national average. So this is not a slow down, take two years, whatever. No, no. Most people need to put food on the plate, so it's a slow down at first. And we as product people should understand this. You want to think about your strategy. You want to understand the marketplace, your customer, the product market fit. You're not going to just go... (00:22:59): You're going to iterate. First step, what do you want and what don't you want? That's the Mnookin two-pager named after Allison Mnookin, who was a member of one of our product councils. So we run product councils and general management CEO councils for people in jobs. That's a paid program that companies pay for. It's out of that program helping those people that I developed this methodology that we're now as a community giving to the world. So Allison, she was the GM at Intuit, and then she spun out a division and ran it as CEO, and she's now a professor at the Harvard Business School. And about 15 years ago, she was in transition and we talked and she created and we created this thing we called now the Mnookin two-pager. I told her, "Allison, I'm going to make your name famous." That's my job. I love her.
turns.zh: 候选人市场契合大概是书里最重要的求职战术，除了求职委员会之外，而且它可能是我以之成名的东西。等我死的时候，他们会在硬币上刻"候选人市场契合"。所以事情是这样的，而这也是为什么它在下行市场如此重要：当你找工作时，你处在一个有供需特征的市场里。所以如果供给很多——现在科技圈就是，因为有很多裁员，而整体经济虽然有净岗位增加，Lenny，但那些主要在医疗和政府。科技圈是净岗位减少。我们可以聊为什么，但这就是我们所处的世界。(00:21:17)：假设你是个产品总监。两年前科技经济和市场都好的时候，你可能拿到产品副总裁的职位。今天呢？今天你的候选人市场契合被压低了，因为有一堆产品副总裁会去接受一个总监角色。猜怎么着？那意味着你可能拿不到总监角色，你可能需要拿高级经理角色之类。现在，这事的重点是，这不是关于你个人的评判。是市场。这就是为什么今天那么多人在给我的留言里说，知道这跟自己无关是一种解脱。(00:21:59)：所以我让人们做的，我让他们迈出的第一个激进步骤，是想想自己想要什么、不想要什么。现在，你可能不觉得这是个激进步骤，Lenny，但大多数人不会做。当他们被裁，他们"广撒网、碰运气"。典型的是"让我就……"等一下，先停一下。他们说"哦，别拖慢我。"我说"我要拖慢你，好让你更快"。事实上，我们的数据显示，求职委员会里从开始到结束平均求职是三个月。如果你看全国的求职数据，是三到六个月。所以我们处于全国平均的低端。所以这不是"慢下来、花两年"之类的。不。大多数人需要吃饭，所以起初是慢下来。而我们作为产品人应该理解这个。你想思考你的战略。你想理解市场、你的客户、产品市场契合。你不会就直接冲出去……(00:22:59)：你会迭代。第一步，你想要什么、不想要什么？那就是 Mnookin 两页纸（Mnookin two-pager），以 Allison Mnookin 命名，她是我们一个产品委员会的成员。我们为有工作的人运营产品委员会和综合管理 CEO 委员会。那是个公司付费的项目。正是从那个帮助那些人的项目里，我发展出了这套方法论，现在作为社区免费给全世界。所以 Allison，她曾是 Intuit 的 GM，后来分拆出一个部门并作为 CEO 运营，现在她是哈佛商学院的教授。大约 15 年前她在转型期，我们聊了，一起创建了现在我们叫 Mnookin 两页纸的东西。我告诉她："Allison，我要让你的名字出名。"那是我的工作。我爱她。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great name.
turns.zh: 好名字。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: She's wonderful. And it's just a simple thing, what do you, what don't you like and you create it and then you share it in your council. And here's something cool, Lenny. Let's say you and I are in a Job Search Council. You share yours, I share your mine. Now you see a few things about what you don't like. I'm like, "Hot damn, I also don't like those. I forgot, I got to add that." Or you say a thing about what you like, you're like, "Oh, wow, no, that's really important to me, and I left that out." So that's part of the shared learning environment. I'm asking you to do these, but with others who you're walking it through. (00:24:16): Now, once you have done that Mnookin two-pager, and it's a draft, you don't have to get it fine, and not everyone knows exactly what they want, by the way, this is important, especially younger people. But sometimes mid-career people too, they're like, "Oh, I'm not... " So I'm not asking you to make a final decision, no, no. We're going to iterate. Okay, we're product people, we're going to iterate. (00:24:38): So we're going to take this Mnookin two-pager, this draft that shared with our council, and we're going to go out and do a listening tour. Because guess what? In the job search, we're the product. We're our skills and experience. That's the product that we're bringing to market. So we have to go see what the market wants. Now we have a sense of what we want, but what does the market want and what does some of our trusted friends, what do they think about what I want and what I'm a fit for? And what do they think I'm a fit for now given the market conditions that we have? (00:25:09): I will tell you, people are terrified to do the listening tour. They're like, "I don't know, what am I going to hear from people?" Because I asked them to ask a golden question, if you were in my shoes, how would you approach this? I call that the golden question. It's such a creative question. It really opens the conversation. But they think, "Oh no, people are going to tell me all this stuff." No, mostly people tell you this. Once in a while you get a helpful piece of critique, "Oh, you make everything a priority, in which case nothing is, and you could work on that." Super helpful to know. We all have stuff to work on. (00:25:43): But I will tell you, once people do the listening tour, they're blown away. I mean, the people who are in jobs, they love, they love helping others if it's done well. Because guess what? They're also anxious themselves, and they want to give back. They want to feel like they're supporting people. You actually end up, and we're going to talk about this, but when you ask someone for help while you've done your homework, you're thoughtful, they want to help you even more. They become invested in you. So the secret about the listening tour is that not only are you getting market research customer feedback on your fit, you're also creating a whole group of listening posts, people who are invested in your success.
turns.zh: 她很棒。而这只是件简单的事——你想要什么、不想要什么，你写出来，然后在你的委员会里分享。这有个很酷的点，Lenny。假设你和我在同一个求职委员会。你分享你的，我分享我的。现在你看到几条你不喜欢的。我说："该死，我也不喜欢那些。我忘了，我得加上。"或者你说起你喜欢的某件事，你说："哦哇，不，那对我真的很重要，我漏掉了。"所以那是共享学习环境的一部分。我要你做这些，但和那些一起走过的人一起做。(00:24:16)：一旦你写好了那份 Mnookin 两页纸，它只是草稿，你不必把它搞完美，而且不是每个人都确切知道自己想要什么——这点很重要，尤其是年轻人。但有时中年人也是，他们会说"哦，我不确定……"所以我不是要你做最终决定，不。我们要迭代。好，我们是产品人，我们要迭代。(00:24:38)：所以我们要拿这份 Mnookin 两页纸、这份和委员会分享过的草稿，走出去做一轮"倾听之旅"（listening tour）。因为猜怎么着？在求职中，我们就是产品。我们是我们的技能和经验。那就是我们带向市场的产品。所以我们得去看看市场想要什么。现在我们对想要的有了感觉，但市场想要什么？我们一些信任的朋友，对我们想要的东西、对我们适合什么，他们怎么看？鉴于我们所处的市场条件，他们认为我现在适合什么？(00:25:09)：我告诉你，人们对做倾听之旅怕得要死。他们说"我不知道，我会从别人那听到什么？"因为我让他们问一个"黄金问题"（golden question）：如果你是我的位置，你会怎么处理这个？我管那叫黄金问题。它是个这么有创意的问题。它真的打开了对话。但他们想"哦不，人们会告诉我一堆东西"。不，大多时候人们告诉你这个。偶尔你会得到一条有用的批评："哦，你把每件事都当优先，那样就什么都不优先了，你可以改进那个。"知道这个超级有用。我们都有要改进的东西。(00:25:43)：但我告诉你，一旦人们做了倾听之旅，他们会被惊到。我的意思是，那些在职的人，他们爱——如果做得好，他们爱帮助别人。因为猜怎么着？他们自己也很焦虑，他们想回馈。他们想感觉自己在支持别人。你最终会——我们待会儿聊这个——但当你问人帮助、而你已经做了功课、你思考过，他们会更想帮你。他们会对你产生投入感。所以倾听之旅的秘密是：你不仅在做市场调研、获取关于你契合度的客户反馈，你还在创建一整群"倾听哨点"（listening posts），一群对你的成功有投入感的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to clarify on that specific point of this listening tour, you write this Mnookin two pager, which basically describes what you want, what you don't want, goals you have, what you hate. And the listening tour is find colleagues, friends, people that are other, say, product managers and get their feedback on what you want, what you don't want, what you hate, what your goals are.
turns.zh: 就澄清一下这个倾听之旅的具体点，你写这份 Mnookin 两页纸，基本描述你想要什么、不想要什么、你的目标、你厌恶的。而倾听之旅是找同事、朋友、其他比如产品经理，获取他们对你想要、不想要、厌恶、目标的反馈。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: And what they're seeing in the market, what they think you're a fit for.
turns.zh: 以及他们在市场里看到的、他们认为你适合什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. Got it. So it's like, "Oh, this is unrealistic. You're not going to get this."
turns.zh: 我懂了。明白了。所以是像"哦，这不现实。你拿不到这个。"

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Looking for that [inaudible 00:27:02]-

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: And we see both things, Lenny. So some people underestimate their fit, others overestimate it or don't recognize that changed market condition. The other thing I'll say is that in the book I have three different kinds of structured listening tour conversations. One I call reverse exit interviews. This is people you used to work with before, go ask them, "Hey, what did I do well, what do you think my strengths are? What do you think I'm a fit for? Here's what I'm thinking. Do you think I accurately am projecting myself?" The second is your broader network, and that's where I ask you to do the golden question, "If you were in my shoes... " And then third is recruiters. (00:27:43): Now, this is an important hack. Recruiters don't like being barraged with, "Get me a job." They do like someone saying, "Hey, what do you think I'm a fit for?" asking their advice. And this is especially true if you pre-
turns.zh: 我们看到两种情况，Lenny。所以有些人低估了自己的契合，有些人高估了、或者没意识到市场条件变了。另一件我在书里说的：我有三种不同结构化的倾听之旅对话。一种我叫"反向离职访谈"（reverse exit interviews）。这是你以前共事过的人，去问他们："嘿，我哪里做得好，你觉得我的强项是什么？你觉得我适合什么？这是我在想的。你觉得我真实地展现自己了吗？"第二种是你更广的人脉，那是我让你问黄金问题的地方："如果你是我的位置……"第三种是招聘官（recruiters）。(00:27:43)：现在，这是个重要的窍门。招聘官不喜欢被人狂轰"给我找个工作"。但他们喜欢有人说"嘿，你觉得我适合什么？"问他们的建议。如果你提前——

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: And this is especially true if you've pre-built a relationship with a recruiter. So anyone listening to your podcast right now, if you're in a job, I have a really important message for you. When that recruiter calls, pick up the phone even if you don't want the job, help them, network with them, introduce them to other people, and build that relationship, because whether you lose a job or whether you decide to start looking when you're in work, you want that relationship. (00:28:29): Now, Lenny, there's a problem many people haven't done that. Okay? So part of what we're doing with the Never Search Alone community is we're building a recruiter network. We're finding recruiters who are willing to, in a protected way, do a couple of conversations a month, helping people think about their candidate market fit. And if anyone listening to the show is a recruiter, please come join us and volunteer. We need more recruiters. I know many of you want to give back and you don't know how. You tell me this. Here's a way to give it.
turns.zh: 如果你提前和招聘官建立了关系，这就尤其管用。所以现在听你播客的任何人，如果你在职，我有条非常重要的信息给你。当招聘官打电话来，接起来，即使你不想要那份工作，也帮帮他们、和他们network、把他们介绍给其他人，建立那段关系，因为无论你丢工作、还是在职时决定开始找，你都想要那段关系。(00:28:29)：现在，Lenny，问题是很多人没那么做。好？所以我们用"永不独自求职"社区在做的一件事，是建立招聘官网络。我们在找愿意以保护方式、每个月做几次对话、帮人们思考他们候选人市场契合的招聘官。如果听这节目的你是招聘官，请来加入我们、做志愿者。我们需要更多招聘官。我知道你们很多人想回馈、却不知道怎么帮。你告诉我这个。这就是一个回馈的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm. Love that. Okay, and so the intent of this is that you're trying to figure out, one, what does the market want, and how do I be honest about what it wants because what you want may not exist right now, and then, two, help you refine your pitch and how you're approaching and who you're talking to. Is there anything else that comes out of doing this exercise? Because I think people might be hearing this, like, "Ah, so much work. I have enough work to do, all these interviews. Got to reach out to people. I got kids and a family. I have to write this two-pager now and listening tour." What other benefits do you get out of this, doing this exercise?
turns.zh: 嗯哼。爱了。好，所以这件事的目的是，你想搞清楚：一，市场想要什么，以及我怎么对"它想要什么"诚实，因为你想要的现在可能不存在；二，帮你打磨你的 pitch、你怎么切入、你在跟谁谈。做这个练习还有什么别的产出？因为我觉得人们听到这个会想："啊，这么多工作。我有够多工作了，这么多面试。还得联系人。我有孩子有家庭。现在我还要写这份两页纸、做倾听之旅。"做这个练习，你还能得到什么别的益处？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: You build those relationships. You turn people on as listening posts, so you light up your network in a way that you... If you just send an email saying, "I want a job," or if you just go, "Hey, do you have a job for me," people don't know what to say. But if you say, "Hey, if you're in my shoes, how would you approach this, and what do you think if you were me I should be looking for, and what are you seeing in the market," they love that, and now they're really thinking about it.
turns.zh: 你建立了那些关系。你把人们变成"倾听哨点"，所以你以一种……如果你只发一封邮件说"我想要份工作"，或只说"嘿，你有工作给我吗"，人们不知道该说什么。但如果你说"嘿，如果你是我的位置，你会怎么处理，以及如果你是我你觉得我该找什么、你在市场里看到了什么"，他们爱这个，现在他们真的在想这个了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And if they see a job that might be a fit, they tell you about it.
turns.zh: 而且如果他们看到一份可能契合的工作，他们会告诉你。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: They tell you about it. Yeah, and that gets to candidate... Because at the end of this, we're going to create a very simple, narrow, focus candidate market fit statement at the end of listening tour. (00:30:17): So once you've now done this listening tour, now you need to create a focus candidate market fit, and this is tough. Look, again, this is why you need a job search council. You need them to be there with you during the listening tour. Not every listening tour conversation will be a home-run. Once in a while it'll be a dud. I talk about this in the book, like, "Warning there are some curves ahead." You could have a conversation... A number of women that I have worked with over the years who've gone and done conversations and they've gotten frankly sexist feedback... It was not helpful. "You're too poised," or "You're not poised enough." It's just this strange set of stuff. So you need your council to help you parse out and interpret what people are telling you. (00:31:02): And at the end of this listening tour, and it never really ends, but once you've done 10 or 15 and you're ready to say, "Okay, I'm going to take a stab at my candidate market fit," now you need your job search council because you're going to want... Every bone in your body is going to want that to be expansive, to want it to be broad. Remember, we're product people, at least those of us in Lenny's podcast community; what happens when we're building a product? Same thing, right? We want this product to be for everyone, but we've learned with product market fit, that doesn't work. We need a narrow, clear focus. Same thing with candidate market fit. So I say to people, and we have this whole grid that we give them, "I'm looking for a director of product role in a healthcare, series B startup in San Francisco," like "Bing, bing, bing," and people say, "Oh, if it's so narrow, I'm going to lose..." And here's the thing, when you're looking for a job, you need a spear and not a net. With a net, everything slips through. (00:32:08): Now, part two to this, people are expansive, but not reductive. What are you talking about, Phyl? Here's what I mean. If you give them a specific... If I say to you, "Lenny, I'm looking for a director of product role at a healthcare startup that's a series B in San Francisco," well, if you see another FinTech startup that's in a heavily regulated industry looking for a director of product that's a series B, you're going to be like, "You know what? Phyl is looking for that, but I bet Phyl could do that." You can be expansive. But if I told you, "Hey, Lenny, I'll take any product job I can," you are never going to think of me. You're never going to remember me. You're not going to be reductive from a broad statement, but you will be expansive from a narrow. (00:32:52): And I'll tell you, Lenny, this is so hard for people, and this is why, again, you need that council and you need that broader community. And every two weeks we do a LinkedIn Live where we address... We go over these questions again and again because it goes... If I were in the job search, I'd feel the same way, even with all the darn research I've done. It's really hard.
turns.zh: 他们会告诉你。对，而这就到了候选人……因为在这结尾，我们会在倾听之旅结束后，创建一个非常简单、狭窄、聚焦的候选人市场契合陈述。(00:30:17)：所以一旦你做了这个倾听之旅，现在你需要创建一个聚焦的候选人市场契合，这很难。看，再说一次，这就是为什么你需要求职委员会。你需要在倾听之旅期间有他们在你身边。不是每次倾听之旅对话都会是满贯全垒打。偶尔会是哑弹。我在书里聊这个，像"警告，前方有弯路"。你可能有一段对话……这些年我合作过的一些女性，去做了对话，得到了坦率说是性别歧视的反馈……那没用。"你太沉着了，"或"你不够沉着。"就是这种奇怪的一套东西。所以你需要你的委员会帮你解析、解读人们在告诉你什么。(00:31:02)：在这倾听之旅的结尾——它其实从不真正结束——但一旦你做了 10 或 15 次，准备好说"好，我要试着写我的候选人市场契合"，现在你需要你的求职委员会，因为你身体每根骨头都会想要它宽泛、想要它广。记住，我们是产品人，至少 Lenny 播客社区里的我们；我们打造产品时会发生什么？一样，对吧？我们想要这个产品给所有人，但通过产品市场契合我们学到，那样行不通。我们需要一个狭窄、清晰的焦点。候选人市场契合也是一样。所以我告诉人们，我们有给他们的一整张网格，"我在找旧金山一家医疗领域、B 轮创业公司的产品总监职位"，像"叮、叮、叮"，人们说"哦，如果这么窄，我会失去……"而事情是这样的：当你找工作时，你需要一支长矛而不是一张网。用网，什么都漏过去了。(00:32:08)：现在，第二部分，人们是宽泛的，但不是缩减的。你在说什么，Phyl？我的意思是。如果你给他们一个具体的……如果我对你说"Lenny，我在找旧金山一家医疗创业公司、B 轮的产品总监职位"，那么如果你看到另一家在强监管行业、在找 B 轮产品总监的 FinTech 创业公司，你会想"你知道嘛？Phyl 在找那个，但我打赌 Phyl 也能做这个。"你可以很宽泛。但如果我告诉你"嘿 Lenny，什么产品工作我都接"，你永远不会想到我。你永远不会记得我。你不会从一个宽泛陈述里被缩减，但你会从一个狭窄陈述里变得宽泛。(00:32:52)：我告诉你，Lenny，这对人们太难了，而这正是为什么，再次，你需要那个委员会和那个更大的社区。我们每两周做一次 LinkedIn 直播，过一遍这些问题，因为我们一遍遍过。如果我自己在求职，哪怕有我做的所有该死的研究，我也会有同感。这真的很难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you've been using this metaphor, approaching this like a product person, and this is very much like a product person thinks about new products is there should be a very narrow audience to start with kind of a wedge or an ICP. When someone's building this, what is a sign they've narrowed it enough? Are there a certain number of attributes? What tells you that, "Cool, this is small now"?
turns.zh: 如果你一直用这个比喻、像产品人那样切入，而这非常像一个产品人思考新产品——应该先有一个非常窄的受众，一种楔子或 ICP（理想客户画像）。当有人在建这个时，什么迹象说明他们已经窄得够了？是有一定数量的属性吗？什么告诉你"酷，现在它小了"？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: So it's typically three to four attributes, and we give people a whole grid in a set of examples. So we had a woman who was a designer. She was a product designer. And what her product market fit was, she was looking for companies that either did not have a design team or needed to reboot one. So she wasn't talking about stage of business, or even industry, but that really plants an image in your mind. If you hear about a company that doesn't have design or looking to reboot design, you're going to think of her immediately because after you've done your listening tour and you've created your candidate market fit and your council signs off on it, Lenny, this is important, then you go back out to your listening tour and you tell all those people, "Thank you for your help. Here's the candidate market fit I've come up with." And you also post it on LinkedIn. You tell the whole world, right? (00:34:29): Now, will that candidate market fit change over time? Yeah, we're iterative, right? So if you go and go... And the market is changing. What was true three months ago may not be true now. Two weeks ago the stock market was convinced we're going into a recession, and everything crashed. Two weeks later we're like, "Oh, no, we're not going into a recession," and that affects the psychology of hiring managers and companies. Not just psychology, their willingness to open up, recs and everything else. So things are changing, so you need to be flexible and adaptive to that, which is also why you need the council and why you need to have a good network around you that you've asked for help from and they're invested in you and can be there for you as you try to keep navigating this.
turns.zh: 通常是三到四个属性，我们给人们一整套网格和例子。我们有个做设计师的女性。她是产品设计师。她的产品市场契合是：她在找那些要么没有设计团队、要么需要重启一个设计团队的公司。所以她没谈业务阶段、甚至没谈行业，但那真的在你脑中种下了一幅图像。如果你听说一家公司没有设计、或想重启设计，你会立刻想到她，因为在你做了倾听之旅、创建了你的候选人市场契合、并且你的委员会签字认可之后，Lenny，这很重要，然后你回到你的倾听之旅告诉所有那些人："谢谢你们的帮助。这是我得出的候选人市场契合。"你还会把它发到 LinkedIn 上。你告诉全世界，对吧？(00:34:29)：现在，那个候选人市场契合会随时间变吗？会，我们是迭代的，对吧？所以如果你去、去……而且市场在变。三个月前是真的，现在可能不真了。两周前股市坚信我们要进衰退，一切都崩了。两周后我们想"哦不，我们不会进衰退"，那影响了招聘经理和公司的心理。不只是心理，还有他们愿意开放、给推荐信等等的意愿。所以事情在变，你需要灵活、适应，这也是为什么你需要委员会、为什么你需要有一群你求助过、对你有投入感、能在你试图导航时陪着你的好人脉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to follow us through it a little bit more, when someone is... Someone's thinking right now, "Okay, what are my attributes," what's on that grid, roughly? There's stage of company, I imagine there's-
turns.zh: 就再多跟我们走一步，当有人在……有人现在在想"好，我的属性是什么"，那张网格上大致有什么？有公司阶段，我想还有——

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Stage of company, industry, level of role and function, of course, and culture.
turns.zh: 公司阶段、行业、角色级别和职能，当然，还有文化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a set of options you have of type of culture?
turns.zh: 文化类型你有几个可选项吗？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Basically everyone wants a good culture, right?
turns.zh: 基本上每个人都想要好文化，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah, exactly. So culture.
turns.zh: 对，对，对，正是。所以文化。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Sometimes it can be very specific, like, I need a company that has a particular kind of policy for kids, or whatever, remote or hybrid or whatever, that kind of element. But I tell people, make it simple. This should not be paragraphs and paragraphs. It should be a one-sentence statement. You can do a longer thing that you can then share with people when you're getting into the conversation, but you want something simple that people go, "Oh, Lenny looking for a chief product officer role. Oh."
turns.zh: 有时它可以非常具体，比如我需要一家对有孩子政策有特定要求的公司，或远程、混合之类。但我告诉人们，简单点。这不应该是成段成段的文字。应该是一句话的陈述。你可以写一个更长的东西，在进行对话时分享给别人，但你想要个简单的、让人们"哦，Lenny 在找首席产品官职位。哦。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's exactly like you want your product to feel too.
turns.zh: 对。这恰恰像你希望你的产品给人的感觉。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I need a SOC 2 compliance, so I'm going to think of-
turns.zh: 我需要一个 SOC 2 合规，所以我会想到——

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: That's [inaudible 00:36:17].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Okay, so I'm thinking through this list here. So level and role I imagine people get a pretty good sense of where they want to be. Stage, any advice for someone to decide what stage is right for them?
turns.zh: 对，正是。好，所以我在过这个清单。所以级别和角色，我想人们对自己想去哪大致有数。阶段，对决定什么阶段适合自己有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: If I were coaching someone which, as you know, I do, we would talk a lot about this. But when I'm in the book and in the community, I say, "To figure out stage again, I want you to rely on your job search council and your network and your own experience," and it becomes pretty... People usually have a pretty good sense, like, "Who was I talking to recently? I need a big..." Whereas many people are like, "I don't want that. I want a startup." Okay. (00:37:01): And what I will tell you is that one thing to keep in mind right now is that there are more jobs in the startup world than there are in the established companies in the tech world for product people. That's where new job creation has been happening. It's slower than it was before, but the big companies, they've just been shedding people. They've just been throwing them off. Whereas the smaller companies, there's more opportunity there. Now that doesn't mean that... If you can't stand working at a startup, I'm not telling you you should go there necessarily. (00:37:35): But I will say this, and again, if you need to put food on the table... We were talking to someone recently; they had moved to a new city and then were laid off the next day. They moved for the company, and then they were laid off the next day, and they're like, "Okay, I need to get a job." I said, "Okay, yeah, sure. Just know that if you're going to get any job just to have while you still look for the job you really want, just know that that's hard. That's a hard pen. I understand it and I support it, it makes sense, and it's hard." It's harder than you realize, and you absolutely have to keep your job search council, because otherwise you're going to get lost. (00:38:16): Can I share one story about candidate market fit-
turns.zh: 如果我在做教练——你知道我会——我们会大量聊这个。但当我在书里和社区里，我说："要再搞清楚阶段，我想让你依靠你的求职委员会、你的人脉和你自己的经验，"它变得相当……人们通常很有数，像"我最近在和谁聊？我需要个大……"而很多人是"我不想要那个。我想要创业公司。"好。(00:37:01)：我要告诉你的是，现在要记住一件事：对产品人来说，创业公司世界的岗位比老牌科技公司多。新岗位创造发生在那里。它比以前慢，但大公司在不断甩人。他们就是把人扔掉。而小公司，机会更多。这不代表……如果你受不了在创业公司工作，我不是说你非得去。(00:37:35)：但我要说这个，再次，如果你需要把食物摆上桌……我们最近和一个人聊；他搬到一个新城市，第二天就被裁了。他为公司搬的，然后第二天被裁，他想"好，我得找份工作。"我说"好，当然。只要知道，如果你只是为了在还在找真正想要的工作时先有份工作而接受任何工作，要知道那很难。那是个难啃的点心。我理解也支持，这有道理，而且它难。"它比你想的难，而你绝对必须保留你的求职委员会，否则你会迷失。(00:38:16)：我能分享一个关于候选人市场契合的故事吗——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 请说。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: ... that might be helpful to people? I was coaching... He was an EVP at a traditional media company, but on the digital side, running their streaming business, but it was very much an old economy, old media company. This was not a player in the streaming space. And they smartly recognized that if they stayed there, they were going to end up in a pretty bad cul-de-sac. And by the way, that company's had layoffs, and they would've... So they decided they wanted to go work for a company like Netflix or Apple TV. And they're someone who ran hundreds of people, corner office, limo, first-class, you know what I mean, in the airplane? What was their candidate market fit? They went out and did this, their candidate market fit, if they were going to join a top streamer was as an individual contributor, Lenny. Because those guys, they didn't respect much of what they brought from traditional media. And if he had done this search alone, he would not have done that. But to his credit, he decided to take that, and it transformed his career. He's not someone who had a lot of management experience, but also tied now with one of the top streamers. He's just done incredibly well. But that is really hard to do.
turns.zh: ……可能对人们有帮助？我在做教练……他是一家传统媒体公司的 EVP，但在数字侧，运营他们的流媒体业务，但它其实是个老经济、老媒体公司。这不是流媒体领域的玩家。他们明智地认识到，如果留在那里，他们会陷入一个相当糟糕的死胡同。顺便说，那家公司有过裁员，他们本会被……所以他们决定想去像 Netflix 或 Apple TV 这样的公司工作。而他是管几百号人、有角落办公室、有豪车、飞机上坐头等舱的人，你懂我意思？他的候选人市场契合是什么？他走出去做了这个，他的候选人市场契合——如果他要加入一个顶级流媒体——是作为个人贡献者（IC），Lenny。因为那些人，他们不太尊重他从传统媒体带来的东西。而如果他是独自做这个搜索，他不会那么做。但值得称赞的是，他决定接受那个，它改变了他的职业。他不是个有很多管理经验的人，但现在和一家顶级流媒体绑在一起了。他做得好得不可思议。但那真的很难做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in this example, when you talk about candidate market fit, a big part of it is what the market wants from you. It's not like he's like, "I'm going to go IC." He just realized as he was going through the process, "This is where I'm actually going to succeed."
turns.zh: 所以在这个例子里，当你谈候选人市场契合，很大一部分是市场在向你要求什么。不是他"我要去做 IC"。他是在过程中逐渐意识到"这是我真正能成功的地方"。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: He talked to people, and I helped him network with people in Silicon Valley. They were just honest with him. And that's what Justin was talking about, this can be hard and humiliating at times to figure out... We had another person who was a chief product officer in a startup, and she was great. She helped me with the book, she was an early reader, she's a member of your community, Lenny. And she realized that she wasn't getting the right product trend. She was the only product person, and she didn't really know what she was doing. Well, what was her candidate market fit? It was an IC. It was an IC role, an individual contributor role in a larger tech company. And to her credit, she realized that was the right path for her learning, and she did this before the shoot really hit the fan. I'm in the tech world, fortunately. Just not swear. (00:40:38): I talk about this in the book. Sometimes you need a two-step strategy. Let's say you want to be a VP of product at a top streaming company or whatever it is, but you not a fit for that today. So the question is how do you step there? I tell a story in the book about a guy who'd been a VP of product. He wanted a COO role. He was not a fit. He was not a fit, Lenny. And it was very clear. The market was telling him, he did the listening tour, but he came back to me and said, "I don't care. I want a COO role." So he interviewed with 50 companies. 50. Can you imagine? It took them a year and a half. The 50th company hired him. (00:41:15): 10 days later, they were a public company, massive fraud, and they went bankrupt. I said, "Okay. The market is clear. The only COO role you're a fit for is a company that's about to go bankrupt." And he's like, "Okay," and he went back to the VP of product role. I said, "If you want to become a COO from that role, where you are today, one of the great paths is to do it from that job inside a company." Okay? And that's what he ended up doing. It was a two-step strategy. He couldn't go straight there. (00:41:46): I'm not talking about people's innate worth, Lenny. I believe every human is worthwhile person, and I deeply believe in belonging and giving people support and spreading love and creating community. But I also believe in being practical and realistic. I didn't create this situation. I'm just trying to report to you what the situation is and how you can manage it so that you don't get stuck. How many people have you seen, Lenny, who get stuck? They get stuck in a bad job, they're not learning, and then they can't go from there? They get into their 40s and 50s, and it is tough. A number of people in the job search community who are in their 50s, 60s, whatever, they're dealing with ageism, they're dealing with... They're not close enough to the technology frontier. You got to get closer to the technology frontier, even if that means you're going to go from the EVP to an IC role. That's how creative destruction works. The closer you are to the technology frontier, the more new jobs and opportunities there are. The further you are from the technology frontier, the worse you're going to be over the long run. You might be able to get a better-sounding job in the short term, but you're going to find yourself stuck.
turns.zh: 他和人聊了，我帮他和在硅谷的人network。他们对他很诚实。那就是 Justin 说的——这有时可能很难、很屈辱，去搞清楚……我们还有另一个人，是家创业公司的首席产品官，她很棒。她帮我写了书，是早期读者，是你社区的成员，Lenny。她意识到她没走对产品趋势。她是唯一的产品人，不太知道自己做什么。那她的候选人市场契合是什么？是 IC。是一个大科技公司的 IC（个人贡献者）角色。值得称赞的是，她意识到那是对她学习正确的路径，而且她在 shit 真正 hit the fan 之前做了这个。我在科技圈，幸好。只是不说脏话。(00:40:38)：我在书里聊这个。有时你需要两步走战略。假设你想去顶级流媒体公司当产品副总裁什么的，但你今天并不契合。所以问题是怎么走到那？我在书里讲一个故事，关于一个曾经是产品副总裁的人。他想当 COO。他不契合。他不契合，Lenny。而且很清楚。市场在告诉他，他做了倾听之旅，但他回来跟我说"我不管。我要 COO 职位。"所以他面了 50 家公司。50 家。你能想象吗？花了一年半。第 50 家公司雇了他。(00:41:15)：10 天后，他们是一家上市公司，巨大欺诈，然后破产了。我说"好。市场很清楚了。你唯一契合的 COO 职位，是一家快破产的公司。"他说"好，"然后回到产品副总裁角色。我说"如果你想从那个角色、从你今天的位置成为 COO，伟大的路径之一是从公司内部的那个职位做起。"好？而他最终那么做了。那是两步走战略。他没法直接到那。(00:41:46)：我不是在谈人们的内在价值，Lenny。我相信每个人都是有价值的，我深深相信归属、给人支持、传播爱、建立社区。但我也相信务实和现实。我没制造这个局面。我只是想向你报告局面是什么、以及你怎么管理它才能不卡住。Lenny，你见过多少卡住的人？他们卡在糟糕的工作里，学不到东西，然后从那里走不出来？他们到了四五十岁，很难。求职社区里一些五六十岁的人，他们在应对年龄歧视，他们在应对……他们离技术前沿不够近。你得离技术前沿更近，哪怕那意味着你从 EVP 降到 IC 角色。创造性破坏就是这么运作的。你离技术前沿越近，新的工作和机会越多。你离技术前沿越远，长期看你会越糟。你也许短期能拿到听起来更好的工作，但你会发现自己卡住了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love your Venn diagram of just warmth and support and belonging, and also just straight real-talk. Here's the reality.
turns.zh: 我爱你的韦恩图——温暖、支持、归属，还有直白的实话。这就是现实。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a combo.
turns.zh: 多棒的组合。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Oh, thank you.
turns.zh: 哦，谢谢你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such powerful advice, and I think people might be feeling like, "Yeah, I get it, but man, I don't want to be a IC again. I've been a director, I've been a VP. That sounds really not great." Is there anything else you can share to help people get past that, of like, "Okay, maybe I really should be looking for an IC role again?"
turns.zh: 这是如此有力的建议，我觉得人们可能会想："对，我懂，但天，我不想再当 IC 了。我当过总监、当过 VP。那听起来真的很不好。"你还能分享什么帮人们跨过那个，像"好，也许我真的该再找份 IC 角色？"

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Again, if you're in a job search council, and also you're in our Slack community, what you're going to find is that you're not alone. That's a big thing. It's not you. There's not something wrong with you. This is the market that we're in. And by the way, the more relationships you build, the better you do your listening tour... One of the tactics, Lenny, I tell people is you've got to send out an update note every month to all of your network that you've talked to. And it might be, "I don't have a job yet," or "I don't even have any news, but I just want to let you know I'm still going and I appreciate everything you've done for me and I'm still looking for X." That could be it. And Justin, in his note, I referenced him earlier as chief product officer, his note on LinkedIn today said, "Phyl told me to keep people updated, and I didn't do it enough." Don't make that mistake. You got to do that. (00:44:12): Lenny, I met with a group of about 50 job seekers recently who've been in the Never Search Alone community for more than a year. Okay? They're struggling. Again, I don't have a magic wand. But as I talked to them, what was happening? They stopped network. They left their job search council. They weren't updating their candidate market fit to the changing market condition. I'm like, "You have to do everything. You can't get passive." One of the concepts, Lenny, I talk about is you've got to be the I in village. There's no I in team. Well, there is an I in village, okay? And the I in village is that when I'm saying you've got to ask for help, you got to be a part of job search council community, you have to be independent and accountable and responsible. I'm not saying you're not going to become passive independent. This is how you become more independent. This is how you stand up and be even more accountable and responsible. This is how you can do the best search possible in the market conditions that we have.
turns.zh: 再次，如果你在求职委员会、也在我们的 Slack 社区，你会发现你不是一个人。那是大事。不是你。不是你有什么问题。这是我们所处的市场。而且，顺便说，你建立的关系越多，你的倾听之旅做得越好……一个战术，Lenny，我告诉人们的是，你必须每个月给你聊过的所有人脉发一封更新信（update note）。它可能只是"我还没工作"，或"我甚至没任何消息，但我只想让你知道我还在继续、我感激你为我做的一切、我还在找 X"。可以就这么简单。而 Justin，我前面提到的那位首席产品官，他今天在 LinkedIn 上的信说"Phyl 让我保持更新，但我做得不够。"别犯那个错。你必须做。(00:44:12)：Lenny，我最近见了大约 50 个求职者，他们待在"永不独自求职"社区超过一年。好？他们在挣扎。再说一次，我没有魔杖。但当我跟他们聊，发生了什么？他们停止了network。他们离开了求职委员会。他们没有根据变化的市场条件更新候选人市场契合。我说"你必须全做。你不能被动。"Lenny，我聊的一个概念是，你必须成为村庄里的"I"（I in village）。团队里没有 I。但村庄里有 I，好？而村庄里的 I 是：当我说你必须寻求帮助、你必须成为求职委员会社区的一部分，你必须是独立、负责、有担当的。我不是说你会变成被动的独立。这是你变得更独立的方式。这是你站起来、变得更有担当和责任的方式。这是你在我们所处的市场条件下，能做最好搜索的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the advice here is if you're struggling finding a job, this is a solution. Join a council, bring people on board with you, update people on your progress. These are the things that break you out of that funk that you're probably in.
turns.zh: 所以这里的建议是：如果你找工作挣扎，这是个解决方案。加入一个委员会，把人带在身边，向人们更新你的进展。这些事能让你跳出你可能陷在其中的消沉。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: And it will still be hard. It will still be hard. I wish that weren't true, Lenny. Now, I will tell you that, look, what's the difference between now and the dot-com depression of 2000, 2001 and 2? The difference is that we were a much smaller industry then. And people had been in web jobs only for a couple years, where now we've got people who are in jobs for 10, 15 or more years in tech who have never seen a downturn, have never seen a market like this. We've never seen a tech market like this. It will improve at some point, but right now it's tough. And I can't change that, but I can provide tools, I can provide community, I can provide heart and smarts, so that you can get the best job you can get right now.
turns.zh: 而且它仍然会难。它仍然会难。我希望那不是真的，Lenny。现在，我告诉你，现在和 2000、2001、02 年的互联网萧条有什么不同？不同是我们当时是个小得多的行业。而且人们只在 web 工作上待了几年，而现在我们有在科技岗位待了 10、15 年甚至更久、从未见过下行、从未见过这种市场的人。我们从未见过这样的科技市场。它会在某个点改善，但现在很难。我改变不了，但我能提供工具、能提供社区、能提供心和智慧，让你在当下能拿到你拿得到的最好的工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of advice, is there anything else along the lines of candidate market fit before we move on to more tactics?
turns.zh: 说到建议，在转到更多战术之前，关于候选人市场契合还有什么别的吗？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Just that, again, that you're going to resist the narrowness of it, every bone in your body. Just know that that's what everyone is feeling. But go watch... I have this great video online of... He was a VP of product. He was initially masked, but VP of product at Nike. I met him through Marty and Chris at Silicon Valley Product Group. He joined one of our product councils, and then he decided to leave. And he was like, "Phyl, I love you, but this candidate market fit stuff, no. You're wrong. It needs to be [inaudible 00:46:57]." And so he went out and he actually spoke to a bunch of VCs and like, " We don't have any idea what to do with you. You have to tell us something really specific." He was like, "Oh, man." So he went, he's like, "Phyl..." So he redid it, bam, bam, bam. (00:47:12): I tell another story in the book about Dee. She was a chief data officer of a large company in tech, wanted to become a CTO. She had a technology and engineering background, as well as data. She spent a year spinning her wheels alone. I said, "Join a job search council." She figured out her candidate market fit. It turns out she was a great fit for a mid-size regional bank CTO. And within three weeks she had three offers. A year, nothing. Within three weeks, three offers. (00:47:43): So I can't guarantee that you're going to get three offers within three weeks, right? I'm not saying that. Some of you, it might take you six months or a year. And the more senior you are, Lenny, the longer it is. If you're a CEO, it's going to take you a long time, unless you happen to be the CEO of Chipotle, who just became the CEO of Starbucks.
turns.zh: 就是再次，你会抗拒它的狭窄，你身体的每根骨头都会。只要知道那是每个人都在感受的。但去看看……我网上有个很棒的视频，关于……他曾是产品副总裁。他一开始戴了面具，但他是 Nike 的产品副总裁。我通过硅谷产品集团的 Marty 和 Chris 认识他。他加入了我们的一个产品委员会，然后他决定离开。他说"Phyl，我爱你，但这个候选人市场契合的东西，不。你错了。它需要是[听不清 00:46:57]。"所以他出去，跟一堆 VC 聊，他们说"我们完全不知道拿你怎么办。你得告诉我们非常具体的事。"他说"哦，天。"所以他回去，他说"Phyl……"然后他重做了，叮、叮、叮。(00:47:12)：我在书里讲另一个故事，关于 Dee。她是一家大科技公司的首席数据官，想成为 CTO。她有技术和工程背景，也有数据。她花了一年独自空转。我说"加入求职委员会。"她搞清了她的候选人市场契合。结果她非常适合一家中型地区银行的 CTO。三周内她拿到三个 offer。一年，什么都没有。三周内，三个 offer。(00:47:43)：所以我不能保证你三周内拿三个 offer，对？我不是那个意思。你们有些人可能要六个月或一年。而且你越资深，Lenny，越久。如果你是 CEO，会很久，除非你碰巧是 Chipotle 的 CEO、刚成了 Starbucks 的 CEO。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, I know you're creating a page that we're going to link people to, which is, I think... Is it phyl.org/lenny?
turns.zh: 对。对，我知道你在建一个页面我们要链接给人们，我想……是 phyl.org/lenny 吗？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. And is it going to have this template to help you work out your market fit?
turns.zh: 好，酷。它会有所谓的模板帮你算出你的市场契合吗？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: There'll be a link to where you can download not only that template, but all the templates. You don't even have to join a job search council to get all this stuff. I hope you do. Again, it's free. I will say, early on people were like, "What's the trick here? This is free, and you're going to charge me." No. No, this is free. Why am I making it free? Because, one, I can, which is cool; second, this is in honor of my mom; and third, I want to create a private safety net for the ravages of creative destruction. It's great. A lot of positive consequences, but there's negative ones. And I just don't love the idea of charging people for this. I charge people for other things, but not for this.
turns.zh: 会有一个链接，能下载不只是那个模板，而是所有模板。你甚至不必加入求职委员会就能拿到所有东西。我希望你加入。再次，免费。我要说，早期人们会想"这里的窍门是什么？免费，然后你会向我收费。"不。不，这是免费的。为什么我做免费？因为，一，我能，这很酷；二，这是纪念我妈妈；三，我想为创造性破坏的破坏力建一个私人安全网。它有大量正面后果，但也有负面。我就是不喜欢对这事收费这个点子。别的事我收费，但这事不。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And we'll link people to the things you charge for so they can support you and benefit you in other ways, or benefit themselves in other ways.
turns.zh: 我们会链接到那些你收费的东西，这样人们能以别的方式支持你、或自己以别的方式受益。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Benefit them and me. That'd be awesome.
turns.zh: 让他们受益也让我受益。那会超棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about some other tactics. You mentioned this idea of playing to win, and I think within that, there's this kind of OKR in mission tactic. Let's talk about that.
turns.zh: 我们聊点别的战术。你提到了"为赢而战"这个想法，而我想在那之内，有个类似 OKR 和使命的战术。我们聊聊这个。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: 50%, Lenny, of the people who read my book, join a job search council, and follow everything I've described, the people don't do what I'm about to tell you, it is the biggest mistake and miss, and I'm really sorry about this. I'm on a campaign, right? So here's the thing. When you start to interview and negotiate, you've got to be in charge. This is collaborative coaching. I want you to play to win, not to lose. (00:49:49): Now, when people hear me say that, they translate it in their brains into, "Oh, Phyl is saying that I've got to be a ruthless negotiator." If anyone who knows me know that ruthless is just not how I am, at least in this sense. No, no, I'm like, "What I want you to do," and it's a great tactic that we stumbled upon, and it's one of the best tactics in the book, and I really hope we can get the other half of the people who are in the community to do this, and your listeners who aren't involved who decide to join also do this, when you start interviewing, I want you to create your own version of the job description. I want you to do it privately, Lenny, and I want you to create what I call a job mission with OKRs. (00:50:38): Now, most job descriptions, they suck, Lenny. The company doesn't know what the eff they're doing. They don't know exactly what they're looking for. But I'm not telling you to say that to them, just to be clear. I'm telling you, "I want you to create your own job mission with OKRs." This is key. It needs to be with OKRs. Now, your audience knows what an OKR is, objectives and key results, and I assume I don't need to explain that. It needs to be something where you are saying, "Here's what I think I'm going to be accountable for. Here's what I'm going to actually... the outcomes I'm going to deliver," right?
turns.zh: Lenny，读我书的人里，50% 加入求职委员会、并遵循我描述的一切，但人们不做我接下来要告诉你的事，那是最多的错误和遗漏，我真的很抱歉。我在搞一场运动，对吧？所以事情是这样的。当你开始面试和谈判，你必须掌控局面。这是协作式教练。我要你为赢而战，而不是为不输而战。(00:49:49)：现在，人们听到我这么说，会在脑子里翻译成"哦，Phyl 是在说我要当个无情的谈判者。"认识我的人都知道，无情根本不是我的风格，至少在这个意义上。不，不，我是说"我要你做的"——这是我们偶然发现的一个很棒的战术，也是书里最好的战术之一，我真希望能让社区里另一半人也做这个，而你的听众里还没参与、决定加入的也做这个：当你开始面试，我要你创建你自己的职位描述版本。我要你私下做，Lenny，而且我要你创建我所谓的带 OKR 的"工作使命"（job mission with OKRs）。(00:50:38)：现在，大多数职位描述都很烂，Lenny。公司不知道自己在干嘛。他们不知道自己到底在找什么。但我不是要你跟他们那么说，只是说清楚。我是告诉你"我要你创建你自己的带 OKR 的工作使命。"这是关键。它必须带 OKR。你的听众知道什么是 OKR——目标和关键结果，我想我不需要解释。它得是某种东西，你在说"这是我认为自己将要负责的事。这是我将要实际交付的成果，"对？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: At the company that you join.
turns.zh: 在你加入的公司。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: At the company you join. Now, you'll keep it private at first because drafting it... This thing has multiple benefits. The first is drafting it will help you understand and develop great interview questions to ask them to clarify, what is this job? And they'll be impressed by that. Okay? The second thing is, once you've had a couple of interviews, and it's a draft... Now, it's not a full, final thing. This is so important. I want you to pull the hiring manager aside and say, "Hey, Lenny, you're the hiring manager. I've thought about what the role is. I want to make sure I'm understanding it correctly. Can I share something with you?" I don't want you to email it. I want you to do phone call, Zoom, or coffee or whatever. (00:51:54): Lenny, can you imagine how hiring managers feel when they get this job mission with OKRs? I was talking to a senior guy at Amazon who's hired more than 2000 product leaders and others. He said, "Phyl, no one in..." He's part of our product account. He said, "No one in my life has ever done this. If someone did this, it would blow my mind. I would hire them on the spot." And that's the message I want these folks to understand. (00:52:22): We talk about silver medals, Lenny. In the job search, the silver medal sucks. At the Olympics, hey, it's pretty good. You get to be on the podium. But guess what? Silver medal is... It's almost worse than... Because you were almost there. And we have a number of videos and other things where we talk about the difference, in many cases, between getting the silver and gold has been doing the job mission with OKRs. Companies say, "This is what distinguished you. This is what..." We were like, "Who is this person?" They're already thinking about what they're accountable and the outcomes, and naturally they're thinking about it better than I am, which is fantastic, right? So it raises the odds, but it also does something if you present it... (00:53:02): Again, Lenny, you're the hiring manager. I show you my job mission OKRs, and you're like, "Oh, this is fantastic," but you also say, "Oh, this thing you have here, this OKR, this isn't part of the role. Well, that's helpful to understand, but this thing that you don't have listed is." "Oh, really?" Lenny, how many times... I'm going to ask people in the audience to raise their hands. How many times have you taken the job A that turned out to be job B? Everybody just raised their hands, Lenny. So this helps to address that, right? (00:53:35): And then if you get the offer, and again, this raises the odds of getting the offer, it then sets you up to negotiate what I call the four legs of the negotiations tool. This is not hard negotiation. This is something the company loves. I actually say, you get an offer and it's like whatever, $250,000 base with a 30% bonus. This may be a director or whatever, or senior manager. Maybe it's an 800 base if you're more senior, whatever it might be. I want you to go and talk to the hiring manager, if possible. Hopefully not the recruiter. We'll talk about that. And I want you to say, "This is great. I want to talk about money, but before we do, I want to think about some of the things that will set me up to see succeed in this role. I think there's like $10 million of tech debt here. Does that sound right to you? And are we on board that that'll be priority one to eliminate the first day I start the job?" (00:54:39): We had two CPOs, both interviewing at private equity firms, private equity-owned companies, about the same size, SaaS companies. One had tech debt of 20 million, one had tech debt of 10. I told them both, "You got to talk about that in the..." So one talked about it in the negotiation, and the company was like, "Oh, that's great." They wrote a check on day one. Six months later, the tech debt was relieved. They updated the systems. They were able to get into innovation. A year later, they got promoted to a GM role in addition to their CPO role, and then a year after that, they were being interviewed for the CEO role. The other person, where there was 10 million of tech debt, was kind shy about asking, sort of mentioned it, they were like, "Oh, we'll talk about it when you get here," but they didn't really commit, and they never addressed it. One month, six months, 12 months, 18 months later, he's looking for a job. This is the opportunity cost of not being set up for success. (00:55:34): Now, again, don't hear this as antagonistic. We're not antagonistic here. We're trying to say, "What's going to help me succeed?" So one CPO recently was negotiating... I'm not just talking about budget for tech debt or whatever. If you're a senior person, do you think that team needs more training? Do you need to send them over to Marty's workshops, over to my product councils, right? Get them into Lenny's community. The company was like, "You're negotiating the training budget of the team that you don't even run yet-"
turns.zh: 在你加入的公司。现在，你起初会保持私密，因为起草它……这东西有多个好处。第一，起草它会帮你理解、并发展出很棒的面试问题，去问他们澄清"这工作到底是什么？"而他们会对此印象深刻。好？第二，一旦你面了几轮，它是草稿……现在，它不是完整最终版。这很重要。我要你把招聘经理拉到一边说："嘿 Lenny，你是招聘经理。我想过这个角色是什么。我想确保我理解对了。我能跟你分享点东西吗？"我不想要你邮件发它。我要你打电话、Zoom、或喝咖啡之类。(00:51:54)：Lenny，你能想象招聘经理拿到这份带 OKR 的工作使命时是什么感觉吗？我在和 Amazon 一个资深人士聊，他招过 2000 多个产品领导者。他说"Phyl，我这辈子没人……"他是我们的产品客户。他说"我这辈子从没人做过这个。如果有人这么做，会让我惊掉下巴。我会当场雇他们。"而那就是我想让这些人理解的讯息。(00:52:22)：我们聊银牌，Lenny。在求职里，银牌糟透了。奥运会上，嘿，还不错。你能上领奖台。但猜怎么着？银牌……几乎比……还糟。因为你差点就到了。我们有很多视频和其他东西聊这个区别：很多时候，拿银牌和金牌的区别，就在于做了带 OKR 的工作使命。公司说"这就是让你脱颖而出的。这就是……"我们想"这人是谁？"他们已经在想自己负责什么、交付什么成果，而且自然比我想得还好，这太棒了，对？(00:53:02)：所以那提高了几率，但如果你展示它，它还做了别的事……(00:53:35)：再次，Lenny，你是招聘经理。我给你看我的带 OKR 的工作使命，你说"哦，这太棒了"，但你也说"哦，你这有个 OKR，不是这个角色的一部分。嗯，那有助于理解，但你没列的这个是。""哦，真的？"Lenny，多少次……我要观众里的人举手。你有多少次接了工作 A、结果却是工作 B？所有人都举手了，Lenny。所以这有助于解决那个，对？(00:54:39)：然后如果你拿到 offer——再次，这提高了拿到 offer 的几率——它然后让你准备好去谈我所谓的"谈判工具四条腿"（four legs of the negotiations tool）。这不是硬谈判。这是公司爱的东西。我其实说，你拿到一个 offer，比如 25 万底薪加 30% 奖金。这可能是总监或高级经理。或者更资深的话是 80 万底薪，whatever。我要你去找招聘经理谈，如果可能的话。希望不是招聘官。我们待会儿聊那个。我要你说："这太好了。我想谈钱，但之前，我想想想一些能让我在这个角色里成功立足的事。我觉得这里有大约 1000 万的技术债（tech debt）。听起来对吗？我们是否一致，这会是我在入职第一天就要消除的头号优先？"(00:55:34)：我们有两个 CPO，都在面试私募股权公司、被 PE 拥有的、差不多规模、SaaS 公司。一个技术债 2000 万，一个 1000 万。我都告诉他们"你得在谈判里谈那个……"所以一个在谈判里谈了，公司说"哦，太好了。"他们第一天开了张支票。六个月后技术债清了。他们更新了系统。能进入创新了。一年后，除了 CPO 角色他们还升到 GM 角色，再一年后，他们在面 CEO 角色。另一个人，有 1000 万技术债，有点害羞不敢问，稍微提了下，他们说"哦，你来了我们再谈，"但没真承诺，也从不解决。一个月、六个月、十二个月、十八个月后，他在找工作。这就是没被设置成功的机会成本。(00:56:??)：现在，再次，别把这听成对抗。我们这里不对抗。我们想说"什么会帮我成功？"所以一个 CPO 最近在谈判……我不只谈技术债的预算之类的。如果你是资深的人，你觉得那团队需要更多培训吗？你觉得需要送他们去 Marty 的工作坊、来我的产品委员会吗？让他们进 Lenny 的社区。公司说"你在谈你甚至还没开始管的团队培训预算——"

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: You're negotiating the training budget of the team that you don't even run yet while we're talking about your salary? Who are you? We love you, we're going to pay you even more. Lenny, companies love this. And even if you're a junior person, you're not going to negotiate budget, but you can talk about mentorship, professional development, will you be able to attend conferences or training? Again, and this is, we're not hard negotiating this, we're saying, "Here's what I think I'm going to need to accomplish the OKRs that we've already agreed upon."
turns.zh: ——我们在谈你工资的时候，你就在谈你甚至还没管的团队的培训预算？你是谁？我们爱你，我们要付你更多。Lenny，公司爱这个。即使你是初级的人，你不会谈预算，但你可以谈导师、职业发展，你能否参加大会或培训？再次，我们不是硬谈这个，我们是说"这是我认为要完成我们已经一致的 OKR 会需要的东西。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is really cool advice, I want to make sure people super understand it. So an example of tech debt. This person asked, "I need $10 million budget in order to address this tech debt."
turns.zh: 这真是很酷的建议，我想确保人们超级理解它。所以技术债的例子。这人问"我需要 1000 万预算来解决这个技术债。"

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. So it's not like, "I believe we will save $10 million if we spend on time." It's like, "Here's how much this team will need and I will need to be successful."
turns.zh: 我懂了。所以不是"我相信如果我们及时花这个钱能省 1000 万，"而是"这是这个团队成功需要、而我需要的东西。"

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: I'm going to need a check for $10 million on day one.
turns.zh: 我第一天就需要一张 1000 万的支票。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I guess you're right, someone would be shy asking for that. Or that was $20 million actually, that was the one that asked for it.
turns.zh: 我想你是对的，有人会害羞不敢要那个。或者那是 2000 万，实际上那是那个要求的人。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: That was the 20 million, that was right. And again, it was not... Yes, people feel really shy about this, but the companies love that they understood what it was going to take. I will tell you what, if the company doesn't like this, it's a huge red flag. Huge red flag, it means they're not serious. But if you're talking to them, "Hey, I think we're going to need train the team. I'm going to need to hire three more ICs," or the design function is weak, or whatever it might be. And then you're like, "Do you agree? Do you see it this way?" (00:57:37): And they're like, "Yeah, that's right. Good. Wow." You're already like bang, bang, bang. We haven't even finished negotiating your salary. And this is so counterintuitive, Lenny. I'm the queen of counterintuitive stuff. Kelly Marcus said it's counterintuitive, right? But this is as well. People think they're going to lose the opportunity when it actually wins them. Now, of course, if they marched in and said, "Damn it, you have to do X and Y," right? That's not what I'm talking about. (00:58:10): "Hey, here's how I see it. This is the OKRs. I think we're going to need this. Does that make sense to you?" And you're having a collaborative conversation about how you need to be set up for success. (00:58:21): And by the way, if they say, "No, I hear you. I believe you, but no," then you make a judgment decision. I'm not always saying you turn that away. Well, especially if you need a job, but you're now going in eyes wide open. You are not going to be able to believe that tech debt initially. You're going to have to work within that constraint.
turns.zh: 那是 2000 万，没错。而且再次，不是……对，人们对这个真的很害羞，但公司爱他们理解那会需要什么。我告诉你，如果公司不喜欢这个，那是巨大的红旗。巨大红旗，意味着他们不认真。但如果你跟他们谈"嘿，我想我们得培训团队。我需要再雇三个 IC，"或设计职能弱，或 whatever。然后你说"你同意吗？你也这么看吗？"(00:57:37)：他们说"对，没错。好。哇。"你已经叮、叮、叮了。我们甚至还没谈完你的工资。这太反直觉了，Lenny。我是反直觉之王的女王。Kelly Marcus 说它反直觉，对？但这个也是。人们以为他们会失去机会，而它其实为他们赢了机会。当然，如果他们冲进来喊"该死，你必须做 X 和 Y，"对？那不是我说的。(00:58:10)："嘿，这是我的看法。这是 OKR。我想我们需要这个。对你说得通吗？"你在做一场关于你怎么需要被设置成功的协作对话。(00:58:21)：而且顺便，如果他们说"不，我听到了。我相信你，但不，"那你做个判断决定。我不是总说你把它推开。好，尤其如果你需要工作，但你现在睁大眼进去了。你一开始不能相信那个技术债。你必须在那个约束内工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I love that we're getting into negotiation advice by the way, because I was hoping we'd get there. So the advice here is identify something that you'll need to be successful, and your finding is that when you ask for, and it seems like a financial investment as a part of you joining, ends up leading to a better comp for you.
turns.zh: 所以我爱我们聊到谈判建议，因为我一直希望我们到那。所以这里的建议是，找出你会需要成功的东西，而你的发现是，当你要求和——它像是你加入的一部分的一笔财务投资——最终导向了你更好的薪酬。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yes, and I will say that there's less negotiating room today than there was two years ago because of the market that we're in. And the data all bears that out, and we see that. But here's the other piece of data. So I want you to ask for things that tie back to the OKRs that you've already agreed on with the hiring manager. This is how this thing connects together, right? It's like Legos, and then we come to the money and you've had this lovely conversation. You've shown them how much you're invested in succeeding. See, Lenny, the problem that every hiring manager has is distinguishing be someone between someone who is a good talker, and someone who can actually make things happen. You know this, right? And this is true every from individual contributor to CEO. (00:59:50): By doing the job mission of the OKRs, and by showing them that draft, you are showing them. Not telling them, showing them that you take initiative, that you're accountable, that you can make things happen. And then in the salary negotiation, by talking to them about what you need to succeed, you're showing them that you really want to succeed. And guess who that benefits? That benefits the company, obviously. I want you to do that first and then, okay, so then let's talk money. Now, 87% of the time, Lenny, when you ask for more money, you get it. Now, that's a longitudinal statistic, meaning over many years. It's going to be lower in a moment like this, but you can still ask, and people are afraid to ask. Again, don't ask in some shark way like some of my friends in business might do. Some M&A negotiators, whatever. No, ask, are you open? (01:00:48): Unless it's a deal breaker. If it's a deal breaker, just be open about that. But if it's not, let's say they offered you whatever it is. 400 base with up to 100% whatever in some RSUs or options, blah, blah, and you really wanted 450. Lenny, you can say, "Hey, are you open to 450? That was really what I was hoping for. What I think I'm worth, are you open to that? Is that something we can talk about?" (01:01:16): And most of the time they say yes. They may not get you to 450. They may be like, "You know what? Yes, thank you. Let me get back to you." Or, "No, we could go to 420. Does that work? Great."
turns.zh: 对，我要说今天比两年前谈判空间小，因为我们所处的市场。数据都证实了，我们看到了。但这里有另一块数据。我要你要求的东西，得回溯到你和招聘经理已经一致的 OKR。这就是这东西怎么连起来的，对？它像乐高，然后我们到钱，你已经有了这场可爱的对话。你向他们展示了你多么投入于成功。看，Lenny，每个招聘经理的问题，是区分一个会说话的人和真正能成事的人。你懂这个，对？从 IC 到 CEO 都是真的。(00:59:50)：通过做带 OKR 的工作使命、通过给他们看那份草稿，你是在展示给他们。不是告诉他们，是展示给他们：你主动、你负责、你能成事。然后在工资谈判里，通过和他们谈你需要什么成功，你是在展示你真的想成功。而那对谁有益？显然对公司有益。我要你先做那个，然后，好，那我们谈钱。现在，Lenny，87% 的情况下，当你要求更多钱，你会得到。现在，那是个纵向统计，意思是很多年累积的。在像现在这样的时刻会低些，但你仍然可以问，而人们不敢问。再次，别用某些我商界朋友可能用的鲨鱼方式问。某些并购谈判者，whatever。不，问，你开放吗？(01:00:48)：除非那是 deal breaker。如果是 deal breaker，就坦白说那个。但如果不是，假设他们给了你某个数。40 万底薪加最高 100% 的 RSU 或期权，blah blah，而你真想要 45 万。Lenny，你可以说"嘿，你对我开到 45 万开放吗？那真是我希望的。我觉得我值，你开放吗？我们能聊这个吗？"(01:01:16)：大多时候他们说 yes。他们可能没法让你到 45 万。他们可能说"你知道吗？好，谢谢你。让我回复你。"或"不，我们能到 42 万。那样行吗？好。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You make it sound very easy.
turns.zh: 你把它说得很容易。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Here's the thing-
turns.zh: 事情是这样的——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I hate negotiating. Yeah, go.
turns.zh: 我讨厌谈判。对，说吧。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: I do too. And I talk about this in the book and Jason Fried, who you know. Jason Fried's got this great thing where they have all very clear bans, 37signals, well, at Basecamp. He's like, "Because no one's trained in negotiation, how can we expect people to negotiate?" And there's another thing Marty says about my book. He says what he loves is that companies have all of these resources. They've got lawyers and HR people, and you're there alone. (01:01:57): That's why you need your job search council. This is when you really need to ask for help because every bone in your body is going to say, "I'm not going to negotiate. That's going to make it worse," and it almost never does. And again, you could be a jerk about it, that won't be good, but that's not what I'm talking about. I'm talking about collaborative conversation. I'm talking about what you need to succeed, showing them that you're thinking about resources, support, budget that will help you deliver on the things that you signed up for. And then asking, are you open if they didn't quite hit your range.
turns.zh: 我也讨厌。我在书里聊这个，还有 Jason Fried，你认识的。Jason Fried 有个很棒的东西，他们在 37signals（以前 Basecamp）有非常清晰的禁令。他说"因为没人受过谈判训练，我们怎么能指望人们谈判？"还有 Marty 对我书说的另一件事。他说他爱的是，公司有所有这些资源。他们有律师和 HR，而你独自一人。(01:01:57)：那就是你为什么需要求职委员会。这是你真的需要寻求帮助的时候，因为你身体的每根骨头都会说"我不会谈判。那会让事情更糟，"而它几乎从不那样。再次，你可以当个混蛋，那不好，但那不是我说的。我说的是协作对话。我说的是你需要成功的东西，向他们展示你在想资源、支持、预算，那会帮你交付你签下的东西。然后问，如果你没完全到你的范围，你开放吗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. The way you phrase it, make it very low risk to ask.
turns.zh: 对。你措辞的方式，让问变得风险很低。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any specific advice on doing this over email, over phone call, or in person? Is there something you're like, "Definitely do it in this way."
turns.zh: 关于通过邮件、电话、还是当面做这个，你有什么具体建议吗？有没有什么是你像"绝对得用这种方式做"的？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Strongly, strongly want you to do it either in person or over the phone live with the hiring manager. Now, some companies won't let you do that. You have to talk to the HR person or whatever. But as much as you can work with the hiring manager, even if it's to say, "Hey, I just want to run by you some of the things I think I need to succeed in the role before we talk money with the hiring manager," or whatever. With the recruiter I mean, and they'll go to bat for you behind the scenes if you do that. Not guaranteed, but more like.
turns.zh: 强烈、强烈希望你在面试经理当面或电话实时做。现在有些公司不让你那么做。你得和 HR 之类的人谈。但尽量和招聘经理合作，即使是说"嘿，在我们和招聘经理谈钱之前，我想先跟你过一下我觉得成功需要的一些东西"，whatever。和招聘官的话，他们会在幕后为你说话。不保证，但更可能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's totally true because oftentimes you don't really have a specific budget as a hiring manager.
turns.zh: 对，那完全对，因为很多时候作为招聘经理你其实没有具体预算。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to you it's like, "Sure, 450, let's make it happen."
turns.zh: 所以对你来说就像"当然，45 万，让它发生。"

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: That's right. Now some companies like know this and they're like, "You have to talk to the person we designate the internal recruiter," but you can also get back to that hiring manager, and even informally. Again, if you've built a good relationship and everything is about building good relationships, Lenny. I want you to be a good interviewer. I want you to ask good questions. I want you to listen. I want you to present that job mission OKRs. It shows how innovative and how much you take initiative and how much you're thinking about this and how much you want this, right? Every step of the way.
turns.zh: 没错。现在有些公司知道这个，他们说"你得和我们指定的人、内部招聘官谈，"但你也能回到那个招聘经理，甚至非正式地。再次，如果你建立了好关系，而一切关于建立好关系，Lenny。我要你是个好面试官。我要你问好问题。我要你听。我要你展示那份带 OKR 的工作使命。它展示了你多创新、多主动、多在为这事想、多想要这个，对？每一步都是。
