turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: In the book, before you do the listening tour, I ask people to do what I call the gratitude house exercise, which is to think about who are all the people in your life who have helped you get to where you are today? I mean, you could talk about your third grade teacher, you know what I mean? I'm just talking on, I just want you to do that, and I want you to do that because everyone has this idea that they're alone. We have all received enormous help to do what we're doing, whoever we are. Even the [inaudible 01:05:51] was born to a mother, and they did not make it themselves for their first several years of their lives. We all are born of mothers. We all are born as families and communities. Some better or worse. I had a pretty tough childhood, but there was love. (01:06:09): I want you to do that gratitude house exercise, and then it can sometimes surface people that you'll go talk to in the listening tour. Might not talk to your third grade teacher, but you'll go talk to some. Now when you're going into interview, I ask people to take a moment and re-reflect the gratitude house exercise, remind themselves of everyone they're carrying with them, to imagine that they're on your shoulders. All of those people, including your job search council of course, and everyone you've talked to and you're listening to, you're walking in with 50 people, Lenny, okay? Even people who tell me, "I don't know anyone." Now, that is not true. You might not know as many people as I do, okay? That's understandable. My job is to know people, but everyone knows some people and you bring them with you even metaphorically, so that you feel not alone when you're going into that interview. (01:07:10): The other thing I say with the interview and the negotiations is you've got to go do the debrief right afterwards, Lenny. Because we all have these cockamamie ideas about what happened. We think we did terribly when we did well, we think... We need to talk it through with someone else who can help us parse exactly what happened and really where we're at. I had a woman who was a director of product, she was interviewing for a VP of product roles. She texted me after the interview, "Oh, I screwed it up," this and that, this and that, "but they really liked me and we're going to go to the next round." (01:07:41): I'm like, "Wait a minute, wait a minute. Something is not true here." (01:07:48): This is just your own imposter syndrome and inner critic. That's another exercise we ask people to do, by the way, is what we call the inner critic exercise name the critic. Mine is Tub Tour. I was overweight when I was a kid and my dad called me Tub Tour.
turns.zh: 在书里，做倾听之旅之前，我让人们做我所谓的"感恩之屋"练习（gratitude house exercise），就是想想你生命里所有帮你走到今天的人？我意思是，你可以聊你的三年级老师，你懂我意思？我就是说这个，我要你做那个，我要你做那个，因为每个人都有"自己孤立无援"的想法。我们无论谁，都接受过巨大的帮助才做到今天在做的事。连[听不清 01:05:51]都是生在母亲怀里，他们生命头几年不是自己撑过来的。我们都是母亲生的。我们都是生在家庭和社区里。有的好有的差。我童年相当艰难，但有爱。(01:06:09)：我要你做那个感恩之屋练习，然后它有时会浮出你去倾听之旅会聊的人。你可能不聊你的三年级老师，但你会聊一些。现在当你走进面试，我要人们花一刻、重新反思感恩之屋练习，提醒自己所有和他们同行的人，想象他们站在你肩上。所有那些人，当然包括你的求职委员会，以及你聊过的、你倾听过的每个人，你走进去时带着 50 个人，Lenny，好？即使是跟我说"我谁也不认识"的人。现在，那不真。你可能没我认识的人多，好？那可理解。我的工作就是认识人，但每个人都认识一些人，你带着他们，即使是隐喻地，这样你走进面试时不觉得孤单。(01:07:10)：关于面试和谈判，我说的另一件事是，你事后必须马上做复盘（debrief），Lenny。因为我们都有这些荒唐的关于发生了什么的想法。我们以为自己做得糟、其实做得好，我们以为……我们需要和别人聊清楚，谁能帮我们准确解析发生了什么、我们到底在哪。(01:07:41)：我有个产品总监女性，她在面产品副总裁角色。面试后她发短信给我"哦，我搞砸了，"这个那个，这个那个，"但他们真的很喜欢我，我们要进下一轮了。"(01:07:48)：我想"等一下，等一下。这里有什么不真。"(01:07:??)：这只是你自己的冒名顶替综合征和内在批评者（inner critic）。那是我们让人们做的另一个练习，我们叫它"内在批评者练习——给批评者命名"。我的叫 Tub Tour。我小时候超重，我爸叫我 Tub Tour。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I learned that tactic from Julie Cameron from The Artist's Way, she recommends that.
turns.zh: 我从《艺术家的路》（The Artist's Way）的 Julie Cameron 那学到那个战术，她推荐这个。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yes, she's great. Love that book. By the way, it's on my bookshelf back there.
turns.zh: 对，她很棒。爱那本书。顺便，它在我后面书架上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I think I called mine Jim. Yeah, we had a really good episode. I don't know if you saw with Joe Hudson, he has a whole series of advice on your inner critic, and his point, and I'll point to it is your inner critic is always lying to you.
turns.zh: 我爱那个。我想我叫我那个 Jim。对，我们有过很好的 episode。我不知道你有没有看到和 Joe Hudson 的那期，他有一整套关于你内在批评者的建议，他的观点——我会指向它——是你内在批评者永远在骗你。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: I did see that episode. I love it. We all have it. People think, "Oh." Everyone. And that's what I love about this moment we're in too, Lenny. I started in therapy in the 1980s. In the 1980s, you did not share that you were in therapy, okay? Today, we have tennis stars talking about their emotional well-being and their therapy and how they're doing. It's beginning to normalize in some really important ways that emotions, they're not bad. They're actually really important to the decision-making system, but they can go off in certain ways that can really hurt us.
turns.zh: 我确实看了那期。我爱它。我们都有。人们想"哦。"每个人都有。而那也是我爱我们此刻的原因，Lenny。我在 80 年代开始治疗。80 年代，你不会分享你在做治疗，好？今天，我们有网球明星在谈他们的情绪健康和他们的治疗、他们怎么样。它开始在某些重要方面正常化：情绪不是坏的。它们对决策系统其实很重要，但它们可能以某些方式失控、真伤到我们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it feels like these councils are like a lite therapy for people.
turns.zh: 而且感觉这些委员会对人们就像一种轻量治疗。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yes. I would never want to say the word therapy because of course that implies certification and training, but there's a therapeutic aspect to it. I feel comfortable saying that, yeah.
turns.zh: 对。我绝不会用"治疗"这个词，因为那意味着认证和训练，但它有治疗的一面。我觉得说这个很舒服，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So on this gratitude house, just come back to it real quick. The reason that is powerful is that gives you confidence to ask for stuff to believe in yourself. You're worth something-
turns.zh: 好。就回到感恩之屋，快一点。它有力是因为它给你信心去要求东西、去相信自己。你值得点什么——

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Gives you confidence to walk in there as who you are, Lenny. Not as your inner critic, but as the whole good person that you are. And when you show up, this is one of the reasons job search councils are so important because if your anxiety and fear starts to run away and erode at your confidence, it will hurt your interview. You will not show up well. So you're not going to even, even in a down market you're going to get even, you won't even get the jobs that your candidate market fit suggests you're good for in that down market. You're going to slide down a few more notches, or you just won't get offers, and then you're going to get paralyzed and feel like you're really worthless. (01:10:17): And if anyone watching this has been out of work for a while and feels that, let me just tell you, you are not worthless. You are not worthless. I want you to invest in yourself, to prove that to yourself that you're not worthless. You are worth the investment of this time and energy. I'm not asking you to do this for me, I'm asking you to do this for you.
turns.zh: 它给你信心，让你作为你是谁走进去，Lenny。不是作为你的内在批评者，而是作为你这个完整的、好的人。当你出现，这也是求职委员会如此重要的原因之一，因为如果你的焦虑和恐惧开始失控、侵蚀你的信心，它会伤害你的面试。你不会表现好。所以在下行市场你甚至都不会拿到你候选人市场契合说你适合的那些工作。你会再下滑几格，或者干脆拿不到 offer，然后你会瘫痪、觉得自己真的一文不值。(01:10:17)：如果有看这个、失业一阵并感到那的人，让我告诉你，你不是一文不值。你不是一文不值。我要你投资自己，向自己证明你不是一文不值。你值得投入这时间和能量。我不是要你为我做这个，我是要你为你自己做这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You got tingles when you said that. That was a really powerful message. I'm glad you said that.
turns.zh: 你说那个时我起鸡皮疙瘩了。那是非常有力的讯息。我很高兴你说了那个。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So yeah, so we're on this topic of playing to win. And what you just said is along the same lines is just remember, you're playing to win. You're not trying to lose, you're not trying to find-
turns.zh: 所以，我们在聊"为赢而战"。你刚说的也是同一个方向：记住，你为赢而战。你不是试图不输，你不是试图找——

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Not lose, just be really, I just can't say anything. I just can't rock the boat. I'm not asking you to rock the boat. I'm asking you to take charge and demonstrate the power of who you are. These companies will love it.
turns.zh: 不输，只是，我简直说不出话。我只是不能掀桌子。我不是要你掀桌子。我是要你掌控、并展示你是谁的power。这些公司会爱它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I asked a lot of people to ask you what you're amazing at, one of those common themes is really good at just asking for help and teaching people how to ask for help, which was actually an topic for a recent newsletter post by one of my newsletter fellows, Natalie. So let's talk about it. Talk about why this is so important, why you spend so much thought and time on this topic.
turns.zh: 当我让很多人问你"你最擅长什么"，其中一个共同主题是真的很擅长"寻求帮助"、教人们怎么寻求帮助，那其实是我一个 newsletter 撰稿人 Natalie 最近一篇帖子的主题。所以我们聊聊。聊聊为什么这如此重要，为什么你在这个话题上花了这么多心思和时间。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: First, I want to shout out my mom again. So my mom's name, her nickname was Chic, C-H-I-C. Her friends and family and I dedicate the book to Chic, and she started that first council in 1960, and she asked for help. Of course, she taught me to ask for help, and to start councils. And of course, when I was very young, I didn't want to do what my mother said, right? You're not. But I ended up in a bad situation and she's like, "You've got to ask for help," and I asked my high school teachers for help. I was an alcoholic at the age of 12, Lenny, and things were really spiraling downwards. I was no longer living with my mom, there's a whole long story about that. I was in a pretty unsupportive position, and she's like, "You've got to ask for help." And so I did. (01:12:23): And OMG, Lenny. I mean, I was carried by these teachers. And I also have to give a shout-out, and I'm going to cry now to my girlfriend in high school, Karen Kavanagh, whose family had very few resources. They were struggling, but they made a home for me, and I couldn't have done it without them and some of my other friends and my teachers. I worked a full-time job by the age of 16 and I was going to high school, and I was in a tough situation. It was transformative, Lenny. It was transformative. Did I feel like asking for help was a weakness? I did. Did I think people were going to think less of me? Absolutely. I thought all the things that people think, and it is not what happens. (01:13:24): Now, there is a warning here. If you ask for help poorly, and I'm going to define that, it does end up leading to bad consequences. What do I mean by asking you poorly? I mean, if you don't do your homework, if you're asking for someone to do it for you rather than advise and support and give you perspective, we all know that. I get these emails, Lenny. So when I started the product councils, Marissa Mayer was a founding member, right? Marissa Mayer at Google and Miriam Moheed at Amazon. And as Marissa's reputation grew, suddenly everybody wanted to talk to Marissa. (01:13:57): So I got all these random emails from people I've never met. "Oh, I've got software, would you please introduce me to Marissa? I think she'd want to license it or buy at Google." (01:14:08): I'm like, "Who are you? What? That is the dumbest." Of course, I'm never going to answer that, right? (01:14:13): If they had reached out to me and said, "I know you don't know me. I have this small software company. I'm not well-connected, but I would love your advice on how to grow this business and what you would do if you were in my shoes," which I have never received, Lenny, even though I've written about it and said about, I would've done that phone call. (01:14:34): And then if they have said, "Well, can I talk to Marissa?" (01:14:36): I'm like, "You have not earned that yet. That's not a statement about your worth. It's just you're not ready for that conversation." (01:14:48): So you can do it poorly. But if you do it well, if you've done your homework and you're open, oh my gosh. There's four counterintuitive rules here. Asking for help is not a sign of weakness, it's a sign of confidence. It both requires confidence and strengthens it, Lenny. That's number one. Two, it's not a taking activity, it's a giving activity. If you do it well, you're actually being giving to the people you ask. This is really counterintuitive, Lenny. This is what I teach in my product councils. I'm like, "You have to ask for the money." If you ask for help and you're open and vulnerable, you're a smart person. (01:15:27): So at one point, Marissa came in and said, " Listen, I'm developing a new product. I want to present it to the board, but I'd like your feedback on it first, and what do you guys think?" Am I approaching this in the right way? (01:15:37): People were like, "What?" Google was already a public company at this point. Wow, that, they were just blown away. They were so happy to help. (01:15:48): So if you've done your homework and you ask someone who has some expertise in the area that you have, and you do it in this way, "I'd love your perspective and thoughts and how would you approach it?" People feel given to, they feel given to. Here's the thought experiment that'll prove it. Imagine that somebody that you respect comes to you for help on an area that you have expertise. And they ask you in this way, how are you going to feel, Lenny? How do you feel?
turns.zh: 首先，我想再次向我妈妈致敬。我妈妈的昵称是 Chic，C-H-I-C。她的朋友家人和我把书献给 Chic，她在 1960 年开启了第一个委员会，她寻求帮助。当然，她教我寻求帮助、开启委员会。当然，我很小的时候，不想听妈妈说的，对吧？你也不。但我最后陷入糟糕处境，她说"你必须寻求帮助，"我向我高中老师求助。我 12 岁就是酒鬼了，Lenny，事情真的在往下螺旋。我不再和妈妈住，那有个很长的故事。我处在一个相当不支持的位置，她说"你必须寻求帮助。"所以我做了。(01:12:23)：天哪，Lenny。我的意思是，我是被这些老师托起来的。我还得向我的高中女友 Karen Kavanagh 致敬——我现在要哭了——她家资源很少。他们在挣扎，但他们给我安了个家，没有他们、我的一些其他朋友和我的老师，我做不到。我 16 岁就做全职工作、同时上高中，处境艰难。那是变革性的，Lenny。那是变革性的。我觉得寻求帮助是弱点吗？我觉得。我觉得人们会看低我吗？绝对。我想过人们想的所有事，而事实不是那样。(01:13:24)：现在，这里有个警告。如果你糟糕地寻求帮助——我要定义那个——它确实会导致坏后果。我说"糟糕地寻求帮助"是什么意思？我是说，如果你不做功课，如果你是要别人替你做、而不是给建议、支持和视角，我们都知道。我收到这些邮件，Lenny。所以当我开启产品委员会，Marissa Mayer 是创始成员，对？Google 的 Marissa Mayer 和 Amazon 的 Miriam Moheed。随着 Marissa 名气增长，突然每个人都想和 Marissa 聊。(01:13:57)：所以我收到一堆从没见过的人的随机邮件："哦，我有软件，能请你介绍我给 Marissa 吗？我觉得她想在 Google 授权或买它。"(01:14:08)：我想"你是谁？什么？那最蠢了。"当然我永远不会回那个，对？(01:14:13)：如果他们联系我说"我知道你不认识我。我有个小软件公司。我人脉不广，但我想要你关于怎么发展这生意的建议、以及如果你是我的位置你会怎么做"——这是我从未收到过的，Lenny，尽管我写过、说过，我会接那个电话。(01:14:34)：然后如果他们说"嗯，我能和 Marissa 聊吗？"(01:14:36)：我想"你还没挣到那个。那不是关于你价值的陈述。只是你还没准备好那场对话。"(01:14:48)：所以你可以糟糕地做。但如果你做得好，如果你做了功课、你开放，哦我的天。这里有四条反直觉的规则。寻求帮助不是软弱的迹象，是信心的迹象。它既需要信心、也强化信心，Lenny。那是第一。第二，它不是索取活动，是给予活动。如果你做得好，你其实是在给予你求助的人。这真的很反直觉，Lenny。这是我在产品委员会里教的。我说"你必须要求钱。"如果你开放、脆弱地寻求帮助，你是个聪明人。(01:15:27)：所以有次 Marissa 进来，说"听，我在开发新产品。我想在董事会上展示，但我想先听你们反馈，你们怎么看？我切入的方式对吗？"(01:15:37)：人们想"什么？"Google 那时已经是上市公司了。哇，他们就惊呆了。他们太高兴帮忙了。(01:15:48)：所以如果你做了功课、你问一个在你有专长的领域的人、而且你用这种方式"我想要你的视角和想法、你会怎么处理？"人们感到被给予。这里有个思想实验能证明。想象一个你尊重的人，来向你求助一个你有专长的领域。他们用这种方式问你，你会什么感觉，Lenny？你觉得怎么样？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like they value. Like they value my opinion-
turns.zh: 像他们重视。像他们重视我的观点——

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: You feel honored, and you feel excited, and you love giving. Everyone loves giving, it's a part of human activity. And you learn more when you give, of course, because it helps you see something new. Asking for help is not a sign of weakness. It's not a taking activity, it means you're becoming more independent, not independent, and it doesn't hurt your reputation, it improves it. Something I did not understand when my mom was trying to tell me to do this, Lenny. And it took the experience to drill into my head. (01:16:49): And then I will tell you, I won't name names, but one person that you asked, who's a prominent product person who's worked at great companies, right? He said ask him about asking for help. I think he would agree with this. He'd been a member of the product councils for a long time. I think it took years before he really embraced it. I've seen many people, they're like, "Bill, I know you keep talking about this asking for help thing." And I know there's something to it, but it is transformative, Lenny. It is transformative if you learn to ask for help well. (01:17:25): I can tell you about Brad Smith at Intuit who toppled the stock price there. But he was a GM. He became a CEO. He was a GM. He ran a project and he didn't do it well. He lost $300 million for company. He thought, okay, that's over. But they came to him and said, "What's your lesson here?" (01:17:46): He said, "I didn't ask for help. I was pigheaded. I didn't listen to my team." That's a great lesson, and if you really internalize that, then it's worth it because you're great in other ways. And he ended up getting to the CEO role. And what did he do? He joined a council, right? And he asked for help. Boom, boom, boom. Stock price goes up 7X in his tenure, okay? (01:18:08): Kenneth Chenault at American Express. Joins in the 1980s, one of the few African Americans in professional roles there. Ends up as a CEO and chairman of the board. First African American chairman of a Fortune 50 company. You ask Kenneth Chenault as I did, how'd you get there? He asked for help. And by the way, what did he do once he became CEO? He got on a CEO council. (01:18:33): And by the way, who asked for help? Well, this is going to blow your mind if you. Warren Buffett. People think Warren Buffett only listens to himself and Charlie Munger who passed away last year. That guy asked for help. Well, it doesn't ask anybody for help. He asked people he respects and so on, but that guy asked for help. Every single leader I've ever worked with that has done well asked for help. And I have data in the book. 85% of the people get to a senior role credit asking for help to help get them there. 85% of the people in a junior role say they're afraid to ask for help because they think it's a sign of weakness.
turns.zh: 你感到荣幸，你感到兴奋，你爱给予。每个人都爱给予，它是人类活动的一部分。而且你给予时学到更多，当然，因为它帮你看到新东西。寻求帮助不是软弱的迹象。它不是索取活动，它意味着你变得更独立，不是不独立，而且它不伤你的声誉，它提升它。这是我妈妈试图告诉我时我没懂的，Lenny。而那需要经历把它钉进我脑袋。(01:16:49)：然后我告诉你，我不点名，但你问的某个人——一位在大公司工作过的知名产品人，对？他说问我关于寻求帮助的事。我想他会同意这个。他做产品委员会成员很久了。我想花了很多年他才真正拥抱它。我见过很多人，他们说"Bill，我知道你一直聊这个寻求帮助的事。"而我知道里面有道理，但它是变革性的，Lenny。如果你学会好好寻求帮助，它是变革性的。(01:17:25)：我可以告诉你 Intuit 的 Brad Smith，他让那儿的股价暴跌。但他是 GM。他成了 CEO。他是 GM。他运营一个项目，做得不好。他让公司损失了 3 亿。他想，好，那结束了。但他们来找他说"你这里的教训是什么？"(01:17:46)：他说"我没寻求帮助。我顽固。我没听团队的。"那是很好的教训，如果你真内化它，那就值了，因为你在其他方面很棒。而他最终到了 CEO 角色。他做了什么？他加入了一个委员会，对？他寻求帮助。叮、叮、叮。他任内股价涨了 7 倍，好？(01:18:08)：American Express 的 Kenneth Chenault。80 年代加入，那儿少数非裔美国人的职业角色之一。最终成了 CEO 和董事会主席。财富 50 强公司第一位非裔主席。你问 Kenneth Chenault——我也问过——你怎么到的？他寻求帮助。顺便，他成了 CEO 后做了什么？他加入了一个 CEO 委员会。(01:18:33)：而且顺便，谁寻求帮助了？好吧，如果你……会让你惊掉下巴。Warren Buffett。人们以为 Warren Buffett 只听自己的和去年去世的 Charlie Munger 的。那家伙寻求帮助。嗯，他不是不找任何人帮忙。他问他尊重的人等等，但那家伙寻求帮助。我合作过的每一个做得好的领导者都寻求帮助。我在书里有数据。85% 走到资深角色的人，把寻求帮助归功于帮他们到达那。85% 在初级角色的人说他们不敢寻求帮助，因为觉得那是软弱的迹象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: It's literally the same number if you can believe that. I couldn't believe it when I did the data. I was like, "What?" But it's really, and guess what? If you don't learn to ask for help and you're a junior person, you're going to remain a junior person most likely.
turns.zh: 它简直是同一个数字，如果你能信。我拿到数据时不敢相信。我想"什么？"但它是真的，而且猜怎么着？如果你不学会寻求帮助，而你是初级的人，你很可能停留在初级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you say ask for help, what are some examples and common times and uses of asking for help? Because it could be like, "Hey, can you just look at this email for me?" Or is it like, "I'm struggling with this project?" What are some things that you've seen when people think ask for help do this.
turns.zh: 当你说寻求帮助，有哪些例子、常见时机和用法？因为它可能是"嘿，你能看下这封邮件吗？"或者是"我在项目上挣扎？"人们想"寻求帮助"时做的一些事是什么？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: One of the things that Kinshaw talks about is what he calls defining reality. So it's a CEO at American Express, he was constantly just going around and asking different people in the company and outside the company, "How do you see things? What are you seeing? What are you thinking? Help me understand your perspective," right? So that's a form of asking for help, for sure. Okay. (01:19:52): Reviewing my email absolutely is a great form of asking for help. If you're sending a good email, an important email let's say, and let's say you have a history of maybe sending emails that don't get well received, you go ask for help. And by the way, I have a whole workshop where I teach people how to use ChatGPT with some communication models to help you with that email. So there's ways to do that with ChatGPT. But I still, if it's a really important email, want you to have eyes on, right? (01:20:22): There's a woman who became the president of a digital retailer in the United States about five years ago, and then she realized that she had significant technical debt. The project, they were trying to build a new platform, and it was stuck. So we convened what we call a peer coaching call, and I also talked about this in the book. We got three other presidents of retailers, online retailers who had re-platformed and spent an hour, just one hour with her asking them for help. "What would you do if you were in my position?" I mean, bing, bang, boom. (01:20:55): So when people get a new job, by the way, I tell them, do a first 90 days peer coaching call. I want you to talk to people who are in that role today. Not at that company necessarily, but they're a director of product, they're a VP of product, whatever it might be. And I want you to say, "Hey, I'm starting this job. Here's my job mission with OKRs. What would you do if you were in my shoes? What mistakes have you seen others or yourself make that I need to avoid? What should I focus on? Here's what I'm thinking for my 30, 60, 90." (01:21:24): Whatever it might be, I want you to do a first 90 days call. Now, let's say you're a director of product in a job is going well, and you want to get to a VP of product role. Well then, I want you to do a career evolution call where you're talking to VPs of product. "Okay, I'm a director. I want to become a VP. How do I get from A to B? Will you tell me?" And that's another peer coach you call. So these are the things we do in the paid community, in the product councils and stuff. But you can do these on your own, right? And I tell people how to do them on their own in the job search councils.
turns.zh: Kinshaw 聊的一件事是他所谓的"定义现实"（defining reality）。所以他是 American Express 的 CEO，他不断在公司内外找不同的人问"你怎么看事情？你看到了什么？你在想什么？帮我理解你的视角，"对？所以那绝对是寻求帮助的一种形式。(01:19:52)：审查我的邮件绝对是寻求帮助的好形式。如果你发一封好邮件、重要的邮件，假设你有发不被好好接收的邮件的历史，你去求助。而且顺便，我有个完整工作坊，教人们怎么用 ChatGPT 加一些沟通模型来帮你写那封邮件。所以有办法用 ChatGPT 做那个。但如果是一封真重要的邮件，我仍然要你有眼睛看着，对？(01:20:22)：有个女性大约五年前成了美国一家数字零售公司的总裁，然后她意识到她有严重的技术债。那个项目，他们想建新平台，卡住了。所以我们召集了所谓的"同侪教练电话"（peer coaching call），我在书里也聊过。我们找了另外三个重新建过平台、零售公司的在线零售总裁，花了一小时——就一小时——和她求助。"如果你是我的位置你会怎么做？"我的意思是，叮、bang、boom。(01:20:55)：所以人们拿到新工作，顺便说，我告诉他们，做一场"头 90 天同侪教练电话"。我要你和今天在做那个角色的人聊。不一定在那家公司，但他们是产品总监、产品副总裁，whatever。我要你说"嘿，我要开始这工作了。这是我的带 OKR 的工作使命。如果你是我的位置你会怎么做？你见过别人或自己犯过、我需要避免的错误是什么？我该聚焦什么？这是我对我 30、60、90 天的想法。"(01:21:24)：whatever 它可能是，我要你做一场头 90 天电话。现在，假设你是个产品总监，工作顺利，你想到产品副总裁角色。那我要你做一场"职业进化电话"（career evolution call），你和产品的 VP 聊。"好，我是总监。我想成为 VP。我怎么从 A 到 B？你会告诉我吗？"那是另一个同侪教练电话。所以这些是我们在付费社区、在产品委员会里做的事。但你可以自己做，对？我在求职委员会里教人们怎么自己做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Are these helpful answers?
turns.zh: 这些是helpful的答案吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. I think all these examples you're sharing is exactly I think what people are wondering. Just like, okay, I see.
turns.zh: 绝对。我觉得你分享的所有这些例子，正是我想人们会纳闷的。就像，好，我懂了。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Feels like it's not-
turns.zh: 感觉它不——

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Can I share one more?
turns.zh: 我能再分享一个吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 请说。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: That's so great. So Bradley Horowitz joined Google in 2008 as director of product. He had come from Yahoo, but he was initially intimidated. He had a weekly meeting with Jonathan Rosenberg, who was the SVP of product, with Susan Wojcicki. Susan just passed away tragically. Absolutely fabulous person by the way, if people don't don't know her, go learn about her. Marissa Mayer, and also another director of product named Sundar Pichai, right? turns.zh: 我要给你一个和我通常会给的非常不同的答案，但我希望你和你的社区会欣赏这个。所以我最近确实发现了它，但我要聊一本书，Lenny。25 年前，一个叫 Robert Strassler 的商人，开始在一个给辍学小孩的特殊高中教书。他教他们一些经典像希罗多德和修昔底德，专家级，但他们搞不懂。而书很糟因为没有语境，所以他花了 10 年、重新发明了历史书的格式。有 120 张地图。每张他专门手绘，只和前一两页相关，好？每段有平白英语的页边摘要，描述那段刚说了什么。他让世界顶尖学者写两页附录，关于他们的专家主题——他们写过几百本书、几百页的东西，必须两页内写完。(01:45:58)：而且顺便，出版界不愿支持它。他自掏腰包。他手绘地图。他花两年做了个概念索引，不只是关键词索引。而它炸开了整个行业。完全颠覆。他卖了几十万本这些书。它们是杰作，Lenny。它们有"地标系列"（Landmark Series）。Landmark。有新出的。每个产品人，在我看来，都该去看看、看看这本书的产品设计。它精湛，教你很多关于可用性和读者体验。(01:46:??)：我要产品人，Lenny，做数字工作的人，走出数字世界，去看数字世界外的产品找灵感和思考，因为我不想你们都看同样的东西。你们只会造出同样的东西。我爱像 Calendly 这样的工具，我用了好多年，但没人做对直到他们做对了。那些很棒。这答案怎么样？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible. So what is it called again and where do you find it?
turns.zh: 那难以置信。那它又叫什么、你去哪找？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: And it's going to be on the Lenny page. If you get on [inaudible 01:47:12], if you do Landmark Herodotus or Landmark Thucydides, either one, you'll get there. Yeah.
turns.zh: 它会在 Lenny 页面上。如果你上[听不清 01:47:12]，如果你搜 Landmark Herodotus 或 Landmark Thucydides，任一个，你会到那。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God. Sounds incredible. Great choice. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often like to think back to and share with friends or family?
turns.zh: 哦我的天。听起来难以置信。好选择。你有没有一个常回想、并分享给朋友或家人的人生格言？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Of course, we talked about asking for help, and I say that a lot. But I also love, and I said this earlier, books are machines to think with. And as product people, Marty and I talk about this all the time, we have to be thinking. And I coach people all the time, how can I think more? You've got to read more because books are machines to think with. Good books. There's a lot of bad books in the business world, but good books. Good books, thoughtful books. Books that'll help and shift your perspective, whether it's history or science. I read widely, and I want you to do the same. Books are machines to think with. That's probably one of my greatest lines.
turns.zh: 当然，我们聊过寻求帮助，我经常说那个。但我也爱，我前面说过，书是思考的机器。而作为产品人，Marty 和我一直聊这个，我们必须思考。我一直在教练人们，我怎么能多思考？你得读更多，因为书是思考的机器。好书。商业世界有很多坏书，但好书。好书，有思想的书。能帮、能移你的视角、无论历史或科学的书。我读得广，我要你也一样。书是思考的机器。那可能是我最棒的一句话之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. Usually I try to make this fun, but I want it to come back to something practical for people. So to leave people with something they could do this week to help them find a job or help them improve the chances of finding their job, what's something you'd recommend?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。通常我试图让这个有趣，但我想回到对人们实用的东西。所以留给人们一件他们这周就能做、帮他们找工作或提高找到工作的几率的事，你推荐什么？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: I have one very simple thing. Go to Phyl.org and sign up for a Job Search Council.
turns.zh: 我有件非常简单的事。去 Phyl.org 注册一个求职委员会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There we go.
turns.zh: 这就对了。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: It's free and it will transform your search. Is it a good [inaudible 01:48:34] answer, or were you looking for something different, Lenny?
turns.zh: 它免费，而且会变革你的搜索。这是个好[听不清 01:48:34]答案吗，还是你在找别的，Lenny？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful answer. It also is exactly what I would've asked you next, which is just where do people go find the stuff you're up to and learn more about things that we've been talking about?
turns.zh: 美丽的答案。它也正是我接下来要问你的，也就是人们去哪找你做的事、了解更多我们聊过的东西？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's phyl.org and then there's phyl.org/lenny, which has a lot of the templates and things that you referenced.
turns.zh: 有 phyl.org，还有 phyl.org/lenny，那里有你提到的很多模板和东西。

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Final actual question, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太了不起了。真正最后一个问题，听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Phyl Terry
turns.en: That's such a lovely question. So on the Lenny page at Phyl.org, I outline some ways. We're raising $100,000 right now to build a platform for job seekers. It will remain free for job seekers. Part of what I'm doing is I'm doing a speaking tour on AI, and I'm taking all my speaking fees and putting it to this, but people can also make a donation just to that. They can also volunteer. And we're looking for, if anyone's a Salesforce admin, I'd love to have you volunteer with us. If any of you have really good PHP experience, let me know. If any of you are really good at Typeform or Formsite, which is a tool I don't like much. By the way, if anyone from Formsite is listening, your tool sucks. You need to really improve the product there. There's a lot of different ways that you can help, but those are some of the things. (01:49:48): But most importantly, tell someone who you know in your life who's looking for a job, that there's a community here for you that's free, that has all these smart tools and resources and people who are genuinely here to help you and who will help transform your search in this very hard moment. People ask me, "Is this good in the hard moment?" This is born out of hard moments. (01:50:12): In a great job market, it's easier to say, "Oh, I can just grab a job." You need to be more thoughtful in the down market. Now, I think you should be in the up market too. This is our moment to be there for people. This is what. And I would love, so many people still don't know this, Lenny, we want millions of people. We want to help millions of people. We have 20,000 hours of volunteer time already. We want to have millions of hours of volunteer time. We are changing something about the way capitalism works with this community. We are changing this negative consequence of creative destruction that people have just been left to fend with on their own.
turns.zh: 那是如此可爱的问题。在 Phyl.org 的 Lenny 页面，我列了一些方式。我们现在在筹 10 万美元建一个给求职者的平台。它对求职者会保持免费。我做的一部分是我在做一场关于 AI 的演讲巡演，把所有的演讲费都投进去，但人们也可以专门捐款。他们也可以志愿。我们在找，如果谁是 Salesforce 管理员，我爱你来志愿。如果你们谁有很棒的 PHP 经验，告诉我。如果你们谁很擅长 Typeform 或 Formsite——一个我不太喜欢的工具。顺便，如果 Formsite 有人在听，你们工具糟透了。你们真得改进那产品。有很多不同的方式你能帮，但那些是一些。(01:49:48)：但最重要的是，告诉你生命里认识的、在找工作的人，这里有为你准备的、免费的社区，有所有这些聪明的工具和资源、以及真心在这帮你、会在这个艰难时刻变革你搜索的人。人们问我"这在艰难时刻好吗？"它生于艰难时刻。(01:50:12)：在好的就业市场，更容易说"哦，我能随便抓份工作。"你需要在下行市场更用心。现在，我觉得你在上行市场也该在。这是我们在那为人而存在的时刻。这是。而且我会爱，这么多人还不知道这个，Lenny，我们要几百万人。我们想帮几百万人。我们已有 20,000 小时志愿时间。我们想有数百万小时志愿时间。我们在用这个社区改变资本主义运作的某种东西。我们在改变创造性破坏的那个负面后果——人们一直被丢下自己应付。

turns.en: Well, I'm excited to be helping spread the word. Phyl, you're wonderful. Thank you so much for being here.

turns.en: Thank you, Lenny.

turns.en: Bye, everyone.
